speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
That, commencing on Friday, July 22, and continuing for each successive Friday until the end of the session, the hours of sitting shall be from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., and 8 p.m. to 11 p.m., and commencing Saturday July 23, and for each successive Saturday until the end of the session, the hours of sitting shall be from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.;
That the order of business and procedure on Saturdays shall be as for Thursdays (government day), and that the provisions of standing orders 2 (1) and 6 (3) be suspended in relation thereto.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the Prime Minister not going to say anything about this motion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the house wishes a statement on the motion I will be glad to make it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: I think we ought to have one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
As I recollect, on previous occasions when a similar motion has been made in expectation of the ending of a session there has been no debate, but if the Leader of the Opposition would like me to make a statement I should like to point out examples of similar motions which I am sure will meet with general approval.
In 1954 the session lasted for 139 days. Today we are entering on the 129th day. As the rules were in that year, the house sat on Friday evenings during the session. The motion in 1954 was made on June 17 to extend the hours of sitting, the house sat on Saturday, June 19 and Saturday, June 26 and concluded the session on that day. In 1955 the session lasted for 140 days. Then too the rules provided that the house should sit on Friday evening throughout the session. The motion was made on July 13 to extend the hours of sitting and the house sat on two subsequent Saturdays, namely July 16 and July 23. In 1956 the length of the session was 152 days, on July 24 a motion was introduced to extend the hours of sitting and the house sat in the evening on four Fridays and on three Saturdays.
79951-0-420
I would point out that the interval between the motion and the conclusion of the session in 1954 was nine days, in 1955 it was 15 days and in 1956 it was 24 days. Hence there is every precedent for the motion now being made on the examples which I have given.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand why the Prime Minister has given us the history of the past. We in this group are not interested in the number of days we sat in past sessions, the time a motion of this kind came in, or how often the house met on Saturdays. We are interested in only one thing, Mr. Speaker, and that is that the business of the people of Canada in this House of Commons-

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
-be conducted in a manner that will not only result in a proper, reasonable and efficient study of all matters still before this House of Commons, but in a manner that will give to the people of Canada a respect for this House of Commons and for the manner in which it conducts its business.
The house is now meeting for long hours, Mr. Speaker. I think it is not generally recognized that a member doing his job is not just in this house when it meets at 11 o'clock. As a rule I arrive here at about 8.30 in the morning, and I meet members of the Conservative party and members of the Liberal party who are arriving here at about that time. I do not think it is generally recognized how many of the members of this house are on the job at about 8.30 or 9 o'clock in the morning accepting their responsibilities, sitting in committees and taking care of constituency matters. The house meets at eleven o'clock in the morning. It now closes at eleven o'clock at night. That is a pretty strenuous session. For three days the lunch hour is out, and now the Prime Minister is moving a motion to continue the sitting hours on Friday until 11 p.m. and on Saturday from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.
Mr. Speaker, if this motion passes, just what does it mean? That we may be able to prorogue this house two days earlier or three days earlier than otherwise? Is our respect for parliament so low that with the pressure members are now under with their constituency work, research, speeches, committees of the House of Commons; with the most important business of this entire session

Business of the House
still before them, the bill of rights, estimates, the defence department, public works and many others, the Prime Minister thinks he is now holding the name of parliamentary democracy in proper respect and because of procedure in the past, this is a good motion to try to drive through to get rid of parliament?
Mr. Speaker, I have never, I believe, pleaded with a prime minister but I am going to do it now.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
It may not mean much to some who are laughing and interrupting at this moment, but parliamentary democracy means a great deal to me. Respect for parliament is something which has to be cherished. You are not going to build up respect for parliament when you have to consider the business of the people under such an extension of hours and days as is now recommended.
Let me put it in this way, Mr. Speaker, because I do not believe this is fully realized. If you bring parliament into disrespect you lay the ground work for what happened in Italy and in Germany, because it is disrespect for parliament that enables a dictator to move in. Even if it means an extra two days or an extra two weeks, let us give evidence to the people of Canada that we are handling their work in a responsible and efficient manner.
Therefore I ask the Prime Minister whether he will not withdraw his motion which is now before us and have consideration not only for himself, with all his responsibilities, but for members of all parties of this house who want to carry out in a reasonable and efficient manner the task for which we were elected.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we intend to oppose this resolution which, as the hon. member who has just sat down said, shows complete disrespect, almost contempt, of parliament.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
As I argue against this resolution I have no doubt my argument will be given the same frivolous reception which the hon. member's argument was given who preceded me.
Mr. Speaker, this resolution was put on the order paper by the Prime Minister without any consultation, either through himself, the leader of the house or any member of the government, with anybody on this side. One might have expected such consultation, even though agreement might not be possible.

The Prime Minister has attempted to mention one or two precedents which in his mind would justify this resolution. The Prime Minister will be very hard put to find any precedent in our parliamentary history which would authorize the House of Commons to meet for the number of hours per week it will be meeting if this resolution is carried.
Let us look at the situation in the last two or three years since this government has had responsibility for it. In 1958, a few days before the end of the session on July 14, the hours of sitting in this house were increased from 25J per week to 33. In 1959 the hours were increased on June 29-the session ended on July 18-from 31i per week to 37 per week. What we are being asked to do this morning is to increase the present hours of sitting, which have already reached a figure of 45 per week as a minimum, depending on whether we are discussing estimates or legislation, to 51 or 52 hours per week, depending on whether we sit through the lunch hour on Saturdays.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: And that is just the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
That is the House of Commons; and I ask the Prime Minister, who has been searching the record, to produce any evidence that the House of Commons at any time has been asked to sit for 51 or 52 hours per week.
Our present sitting hours of 45 hours per week are unprecedented, and they represent a minimum which in itself is creating difficulties not only for members of parliament but for all those officers and employees of the house who have to serve and cover the work of the House of Commons. It would, I think, be quite impossible to continue our work satisfactorily and accept any increase in the present unprecedented number of hours we are sitting. As the hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out two years ago when we were asked to increase hours of sitting to 33, taking away Saturday meant that there would be no week ends for preparatory work in readiness for the week's business that was to come.
Even if all the important legislation had been disposed of, even if there were nothing but estimates before the house, and even if it were only a few days before the end of the session, we could not support this resolution. But what is the situation with regard to the work before the house and the end of the session? It certainly will not be possible to complete the work we have now on the order paper before at least a fortnight, and perhaps before three or four weeks. In that situation would it not be

better to go ahead at the speedy pace, in so far as hours are concerned, that we are now following until this work is done, until we can give that work the consideration to which it is entitled? Or, if the government is not willing to do that, we might adjourn and come back in the autumn. In any event, perhaps an autumn session will be required because of the serious domestic or international situation.
We have to consider the situation first in the light of the estimates that have not been passed, then in the light of the legislation that has not been passed, and then having regard to the work of the committees; and all three considerations make it clear that we are far from the end of the session, as we in the official opposition certainly propose to discharge our duty as best we can in all three categories I have mentioned, namely estimates, legislation and committees.
What did the Prime Minister himself say about the desirability of parliament continuing regularly in session even during the summer months? On June 14 of this year, as reported at page 4879 of Hansard, the hon. gentleman said:
All I can say in that regard-
He was talking about the length of the session. I continue:
-is that I like parliament to be sitting, because it is very helpful to get the views of hon. members-
The Prime Minister likes parliament to be sitting so much that he is asking us now to extend the length of our sittings to over 50 hours a week so that we can rush everything through in the last weeks of the session. The situation with regard to estimates is that eight or nine important departments have not yet even been introduced. So far as committees are concerned we have two very important committees now sitting, the bill of rights committee and the combines committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: The banking and commerce committee finished on Monday. Bring us up to date.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: What more important committee could there be than the one considering the bill of rights? In addition to this we have an agricultural committee and a broadcasting committee which organized itself only on July 20.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Some organization.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister says that the bill of rights is one of the most important measures that has ever been introduced into a Canadian parliament. It was introduced on July 1 in a session which began early in January-
79951-0-420J
Business of the House

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the applause given to that observation about the bill of rights being in the view of the Prime Minister one of the most important measures ever introduced into a Canadian parliament is in startling contrast to the reception given to this bill in the committee by the witnesses who have been called before it. In any event, of course, it is an important bill and should be given the careful and thorough consideration which was solemnly promised by the Prime Minister when he told the Canadian Bar Association that it would be introduced at the beginning of the session and sent at once to a joint committee. As the Canadian Labour Congress has said with reference to the bill of rights:
Great issues, profound issues, issues of immense legal difficulty, are at stake. It is simply impossible for any individual, however learned, however eloquent, however long he has considered these questions, to present his views adequately upon a few days' notice. It is simply impossible for all the individuals who should be heard to make their views known to you within the compass of five or six days. And what is true of individuals is even truer of organizations, which, in the nature of things, need more time to prepare their submissions.
This is not the way to deal with questions of such import.
The broadcasting committee to which I have made reference has not even begun its sessions yet, and chose its chairman only on July 20. The Prime Minister himself earlier in this session and also last session said he would be prepared to do what he could to ensure that the work of the committees would not interfere with the important work in the House of Commons itself. We know, and especially those hon. members who are working on committees know, how impossible it is to satisfactorily carry on the work in these important committees and to do the work which is required in the House of Commons. The bill of rights committee met in the afternoon when the estimates of the Department of External Affairs were before the House of Commons, and those hon. members serving on the committee had to shuttle back and forth between the chamber and the committee. The bill of rights committee is meeting today at nine o'clock, at two o'clock and at eight o'clock in order to rush its important work through so the Prime Minister and the government can get rid of parliament at the earliest possible date. That is not the way the Prime Minister talked earlier in the session or last session. As found on page 990 of Hansard for February 13, 1959, the Prime Minister had this to say:
I for one will say unequivocally that if at any time there is any action taken that would deny members of the opposition a fair opportunity of
6658	HOUSE OF
Business of the House discharging their responsibility, I shall immediately see to it that a change is made to assure justness and fairness.
When that pledge was referred to by the hon. member for Essex East on February 25 of this year the Prime Minister said, as found on page 1435 of Hansard:
I entirely confirm the remarks I made at that time.
I ask the Prime Minister, will he do something now, instead of bringing a resolution of this kind before the house, to make it possible for the members of this and other committees to do their work effectively in committee and to do their work effectively in the House of Commons?
This resolution, Mr. Speaker, asks us to extend the hours of sitting to 51 or 52 per week. As a result of the ineptness, confusion, delay, fumbling and bumbling by the government in the organization of the work of the session, we are now being asked to accept this motion on July 21. Well, Mr. Speaker, we refuse to do so. No doubt the government majority will pass the resolution, but we are now being asked by the government to face a situation which in effect means legislation through confusion by exhaustion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know it may not be customary for a humble backbencher to take part in a debate of this nature, but I should like to say something about this matter. First of all, I should like to say to the hon. member for Vancouver East that government backbenchers, government ministers, all government members, are conscious of their responsibilities to Canada and Canadians.
I should also like to point out that I come to my office at eight o'clock in the morning. I do not have a staff of researchers to do half my work for me. I do it myself. I live 2,600 miles from here, and I have a family of whom I am extremely fond. I want to get home, and I am perfectly willing to work long hours to achieve that objective. The Leader of the Opposition, who makes a great outcry about the imposition upon the opposition and upon parliament, lives in Ottawa and many of his members live very close to Ottawa. But those who come from places a long distance from Ottawa and who are just as conscious of the work there is to do would like to go home in order to have a few weeks with their families.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Why not have a recess, then?

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
I think the argument made by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Vancouver East is entirely


unfair not only to government members but to their own backbenchers who live a long distance away.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: I live 3,000 miles away.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to repeat the arguments of the preceding opposition speakers, because I agree with them. I rise particularly because of the Prime Minister's reference to the practice and procedures of the past. It is obvious that he had searched the records for some supporting argument for the motion he has presented to the house this morning. I simply want to add in that connection that it is obvious now to all of us on this side that instead of being the Progressive Conservative party, the government considers itself the curator of a national museum.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Are you one of the exhibits?

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: But, Mr. Speaker, worse than that, when the Prime Minister was introducing the motion he reminded me of one returning in high spirits and a happy frame of mind coming from a funeral.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: This is one of the reasons we are still here.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Do you know why he was happy? Because he had charge of all the arrangements. We do hope that the experience this session will cause the government to give consideration to the planning of next session's agenda, to an early introduction of legislation and an adjournment of the house, as we have said before, some time in June and resumption of the sessional activities some time late in the fall. We appeal to the Prime Minister and the government to give consideration to this suggestion. Surely by some planning and logic in our arrangements we can end this tantalizing, tenebrous torture that we have experienced in recent years.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are one or two things I should like to contribute concerning the motion by the Prime Minister and arising out of the interruptions that have been made by members on the other side of the house. One of these is that on repeated occasions the Prime Minister has been very careful to speak of the co-operation which has been extended by this side of the house in connection with the conduct of the business of the house. If there was one occasion on which there should have been co-operation with this side of the house, it was when an additional 10 hours per week were being added to the sittings of the house. Yet not one word was uttered

by the leader of the house or anyone on the other side to indicate that this motion was coming forward, although we have heard a great deal from the other side of the house about co-operation. There is an expression used among French people, which goes like this: "II se gargarise de mots".
All I need say is that I believe that is what is happening on the other side of the house, not only with reference to this motion but with reference to many other matters. They are gargling themselves with words. We saw it the other evening. On Tuesday we saw an example of the confused manner in which government business is being carried on. An amendment to the motion to go into committee of supply was moved by the C.C.F. group, and it was quite clear that the government had completely forgotten that this was a possibility on that day. What was the result? The whole day was lost in large part because government supporters filibustered the amendment in order not to vote on it. There is no doubt about that, because we on this side of the house sat here and made no attempt to participate in the debate-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: You moved an amendment.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: What about the hon. member for Essex East? He spoke for 80 minutes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: -until the minister got back. What did we get from the minister? He said that he regretted very much the words of the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Essex East because he did not know this matter was coming up. He should know the rules of the house. So should the Minister of Agriculture, who was caught in the same fashion, and the Minister of Transport, who was also caught in the same fashion. They were not here.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is illustrating a point which I consider to be relevant, but I think in doing so he is getting into irrelevancies.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Sir, I respectfully disagree with you, because I am discussing the business of the house and I am saying the government is not ready with the business of the house. I am saying that if the government had been ready with legislation on Tuesday, as it should have been, the day would not have been lost in the manner in which it was lost.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Lost?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
I am also saying that on motion to go into supply the ministers should know the rules and should be in their seats in order to be able to discuss the matters that are raised. Therefore I have no hesitation
Business of the House in saying that this motion should not be placed before us at this time.
I say this respectfully to the Prime Minister. It is unworthy of him; it is unworthy of the person who is responsible for bringing about a bill of rights, because we are being forced into submission in considering legislation on combines and on the bill of rights, important matters which this parliament is considering, together with the estimates of eleven departments, no less than eight of which are of great importance.
How can we, in all reasonableness, in all fairness, considering the hours we have to sit, deal with these matters efficiently, seriously and earnestly? What more have we got besides these estimates and this legislation? We have five committees that have not completed their work and are still sitting, and we have three other committees that are standing by to which matters might be referred.
A short time ago the Prime Minister put on Hansard some of the things that happened earlier. I have a detailed statement which has been provided for me. I shall only read one short part of it. In 1955 there was a grand total of 95 additional hours or 17.2 normal working days after the morning sittings, the Saturday sittings and the Wednesday evening settings were brought into effect. During the 1956 session there were 84 additional hours and during the 1957 session, 40J hours. As the Prime Minister has indicated, in those days the hours of sitting were from 11 in the morning until 1, from 2.30 in the afternoon until 6, and from 8 in the evening until 10, with the exception of Saturday. Under this motion, with the addition of mornings and Wednesday evenings, this house has sat for 109 extra hours or 18 normal working days July 4 to July 20. How then, I ask you, sir, can we deal with the important legislation that still remains on the order paper and all the estimates which we would like to consider in the manner in which they should be considered?
We had an example yesterday of another committee of this house which I shall not name but to which a great deal of attention has been given, which sat for a long time and accounted in part, I am told, for the fact that many of the other committees that were called were not able to obtain a quorum. This resulted from the fact that flashlight bulbs were being exploded in this particular committee which sat from 10 in the morning until
11.30	at night, and to which a tremendous amount of importance seems to have been given.
I protest, along with my leader and those of us who are on this side of the house, against these hours which are being added now in

Business of the House order to bring about legislation, as the Leader of the Opposition has said, by exhaustion; in order to make us submit to a program which is unbearable under the circumstances. The Prime Minister has suggested that this attempt is made because one can see the end of the session ahead. Well, I do not see the end of the session ahead, and I do not see that this is going to assist to bring about the end in any way whatever. It would if the greater part of the estimates were completed, but this session seems to have accomplished little or nothing in the way of important legislation because there has been confusion, uncertainty and indecision in the program of the government.
I am not going to sit here and take this motion without protest when I know that we may be sitting these hours for another four weeks. I suggest to the Prime Minister that this motion might well be dropped so we could carry on under the present hours, and perhaps deal with legislation and the estimates in the manner in which the Prime Minister had in mind to deal with them at the outset, in co-operation with the government, so that the business of the house could be conducted efficiently.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been quite a bit of sound and fury from the other side of the house, as if to indicate that there was something new in the suggestion made this morning. The Prime Minister has pointed out examples in three other years when the hon. gentlemen opposite were in office, and on those occasions the house accepted the fact that in the closing days of the session the hours should be extended and the business of the house conducted in an orderly manner, but nevertheless promptly, without compelling people from the distant parts of this country to remain in Ottawa without the house in session on Fridays and Saturdays.
Hon. gentlemen opposite now have a complete disregard for the members who come from the distant parts of Canada. They care nothing as to how long these members are kept here waiting on Fridays and Saturdays without the house in session when business could be accomplished. This is something I know from my own experience when I sat on the opposition side. In those days the opposition was just as eager as the government to complete the business of the house and put in the hours that were necessary to do so.
There is no rush with regard to the business. The hours are variable, and every member of this house knows that. A member does not have to be here every single minute of the time. His colleagues can spell him off,
[Mr. Chevrier.l
and this sort of thing goes on every single day. The people who are complaining now that they have not the time, that they are overworked and so on, are overlooking the fact that they have friends who can spell them off on duty in this house. This goes on every single day, and has throughout the session. It is not just a question of getting home, but it is a question of getting the business of the house accomplished without too much delay.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Why did you not start in March?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition made quite a point of the fact that committees are still sitting, as if this had never happened before. In the session of 1956 there were five committees of the house that were sitting toward the end of July and into August. That session ran into the middle of August. Then he pretends that something new has happened this year. We were under the same pressures when we were in opposition as the members of the opposition are under now. We understand all about it. There was more than one occasion, in my recollection of the days in opposition, when 100 members of the house were engaged in committee work toward the end of the session, and business still went on here in the chamber. This is not new.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
We thought you had a new
vision.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
In 1954 the hours were extended, as has been pointed out, by adding Saturdays and by reducing the dinner recess by one hour. The motion is available and can be read out by anyone who wants to look at it. It can be found on page 6120 of Hansard for June 17, 1954. This motion extended the hours of sitting to about 48 per week. Well, the opposition of that day did not shed the crocodile tears we have seen this morning. We accepted our responsibility and carried on with the work.
The Leader of the Opposition has attempted to make a point about lack of consultation and co-operation. There has been more consultation and co-operation this session than in any session with which I am familiar, and arrangements have been upset by none other than the Leader of the Opposition himself.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the
minister a question? Why was there not consultation with this side of the house in connection with this motion, as the minister has said there has been in connection with other motions?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
There has been very effective consultation. This has been a matter

not of specific consultation yesterday or the day before; it has been a matter of conversation with hon. members on the opposite side of the house as to the termination of the session and when we would start Saturday sittings. As I say, this procedure has been going on for years. There is nothing new about it. It is just a matter of reaching a certain stage of the session where you can see the approximate end, and at that time the Saturday sittings commence. have been reached again this session if the government had behaved in that way. But for some reason or another this whole business of consultation in recent days has completely broken down, and it has completely broken down because the government has not adhered to undertakings that were made-

speechtext:
I am asked by the government whip to name one. I intend to recite all the details of that particular case. At the end of the week before last the Department of Labour was called as one of the departments for Monday. At the request of the minister, who came over and consulted me about the matter, we agreed that it should be deferred until Tuesday. Then the minister took some exception to that arrangement and said he had had conversations with some of my hon. friends, and asked if it would be all right with us if it came on instead on Friday. After consultation with my leader I said that would be quite agreeable to us. It was understood that that was what was going to happen. That was, as I understood it, a firm undertaking, but that undertaking was not kept.
The whip asked for an example, and there it is. The plain fact is that it has been quite impossible to know from one day to the next what departments would be taken up in committee of supply, and that has greatly complicated the work of the opposition; because if we knew for sure what departments were to be taken up in committee of supply it would be somewhat less difficult-only somewhat less difficult-to have the consecutive attendance there ought to be in other committees.
The minister talked about members spelling one another off. I must say that certainly is very conspicuous on the treasury benches, where for a good deal of the time this session there has been a maximum attendance of two ministers and often only of one. There has been an unprecedented lack of ministers in attendance in the house. I suggest that is one of the difficulties, that ministers are paying so little attention to the house and the proceedings of the house, and that a great deal of confusion and disorder in the business of the house results from that fact itself.
But the real problem we are faced with in this session, which we were not faced with in previous sessions under this government and which we were certainly not faced with under the preceding government, is that for half

this session there was no government business before us at all. The government did not bring down, except for one or two relatively trivial or transitory pieces of legislation, any important legislation at all. It took no steps to set up committees, like the broadcasting committee which could have functioned effectively in the early part of the session; and there has been a dilatoriness, a procrastination and a refusal to bring forward the business, and a refusal to face up to problems which I think is probably unprecedented in the whole history of parliament in this country.
Certainly to some of us who have been observing the conduct of business in this house, and to some like the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Essex East who have participated in this house since 1935, it has been quite unprecedented. Now at the end we are faced with a new, subtle form of closure.

We get the most important legislation, the combines act and the bill of rights, undoubtedly the two most important pieces of legislation of this session, introduced at the very last moment. Then the hours are increased to the point where it is quite impossible for members to attend to their business in the house and attend consecutively those two committees which are running concurrently. Consequently it has been quite impossible for anyone to carry on properly.
Some of these backbenchers who talk so much of wanting to get home have over and over again this session, at committees I have attended personally, failed to turn up so there have not been quorums for those committees sometimes for half an hour, as was the case yesterday with the broadcasting committee when the prospective chairman did not turn up for half an hour. As a matter of fact-
Mr. Pallet!: On a question of privilege, the hon. member to whom reference has just been made is not presently in the chamber, and as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate knows there was confusion as to the room number of that committee; so let there be no mistake about that.

That sort of thing is not untypical of what has happened this session, and it seems to me that to attempt at the same time to
Business of the House conduct committees on the most important legislation of the session, and to ask this house to sit over 50 hours and have it rammed down our throats by a majority, if that is not closure you can pick out some other name for it. But it is so near it that for the life of me I cannot see any difference between the two.
A good deal was made by the Prime Minister of the precedent of 1954. Anyone who looks at Hansard for June 17 of that year will see that when Mr. St. Laurent moved the motion to extend the hours and to provide for Saturday sittings, that motion was obviously agreed to in advance by the opposition; because the only discussion about it was a reference by Mr. Gillis, a very proper reference, to the position of the staff of the house. subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS

I do not deny that for one minute, and I certainly do not want to say anything which is in any respect unfair. I said that in the previous two sessions and also in the early part of this session there

Business of the House was consultation, and on a very good basis. But it does seem that for some reason or other in the past two or three weeks it has broken down completely. That is what I am complaining about, and it is undoubtedly one reason why we are having this debate today instead of having reached some reasonable agreement on this matter before any motion was brought before the house.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the fundamental reason we are having to consider anything of this sort at all is because of the hopelessly dilatory, procrastinating tactics of the government with respect to the legislation and the business of the house, and the confusion and uncertainty about bringing forward the government's business.

[Mr. Pickersgill.l

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
The presentation of this motion proves only one thing; that the business of the house has increased so much that it has become a full-time job, and it should be considered as such, as was stated by the hon. member for Port Arthur a few weeks ago. They are talking about members from far away who want to be with their families. I am perfectly in accord with that. I know that members such as the hon. member for Gloucester and others have children who go away to school. They are at boarding school. Even if they get back home by the middle of August they will not be able to be with their families, because the children will have gone back to school.
It may be time to reconsider the whole set-up of the work we have to do during the session. I believe the summer recess is what we should consider at this time. I am not speaking for myself because I am living at home, as some hon. members have said before. What people with families need is a recess while their families are at home or in the country. This resolution will not change anything, because the house will have to sit from three to four weeks longer anyway. By the time they get home it will be time to prepare the children to go back to school.
This being a fulltime job, as the hon. member for Port Arthur has said, it should be set up as such, and it is time the government should consider an increase in the salaries paid to members. There are a lot of backbenchers who might be better than some of the ministers at the present time. They should be paid properly so they can regard this as a fulltime job. This is the case even with regard to the Prime Minister and the ministers of the crown. I do not think they are being properly paid now for the job they are doing.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: May I be permitted to differ with Your Honour on that point, because if it is relevant to discuss the extension of our hours of sitting it is relevant to consider having a summer recess instead of a fall recess; and I think, therefore, it is relevant to consider at the same time the remuneration of those who would be affected by such a change. That is why I spoke of the salaries paid to members.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
I am sorry, but I cannot agree with the hon. member on that point. The question before the house is not really the adjournment of the house for a summer recess. It has to do with the hours of sitting. I allowed the hon. member to discuss the

other subject because it had to do with an alternative method of carrying out our duties, but I think we should not discuss the question of remuneration.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Well, I will not speak any more on remuneration. I have made my point on that, anyway. But there is one thing. Instead of extending the hours of sitting the government should be talking about allowing a summer recess. I know that a few lawyers would prefer to be free in the fall when the fall assizes are held, but that is not a matter which affects every member of this house. If the aim of the Prime Minister is to exhaust members of parliament so the business of the house may go faster, I think we should consider amending the present motion so it would read "Commencing on Friday, July 22 and continuing until the end of the present session, the days of sitting shall be Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and so on, and the hours of sitting shall be from 7 a.m. until 12 midnight, and that the committees shall have the right to sit from 12 midnight until 7 a.m. every day until the end of the session, and that rules 66 and 67 be suspended accordingly".
I think then the Prime Minister would have it completely made, and at the end of the session he could bring in a new bill, not a bill of rights but a bill of rest to give hon. members a chance to take a breath.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS

Mr. Speaker, there are one or two things which should be said to restore a sense of proportion to this discussion because of the grossly exaggerated things which have been said by members of the opposition.
I do not suppose it really advances the debate very much to get into a catalogue of all the minor incidents which could be brought up to indicate that this or that accommodation has been made and broken, and this or that misunderstanding has arisen, although that is the tactic which members opposite, particularly the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, have sought to follow. But since the opposition are making such point of the accusation that there has been lack of efficiency and lack of consideration for members opposite on the part of the government, I think it is only appropriate to ask them to remind themselves that this sort of thing has happened before.
This sort of charge has been made before. This sort of problem has arisen at this stage of other sessions. Indeed, as I recall it on the basis of some 15 years' experience-it is true that other hon. members have been here longer-it is the rare session when heated things are not said about the extension of the hours of sitting or about understandings
Business of the House and misunderstandings that arise when the house is attempting to finish up its business.
I should hope that if hon. members opposite would recall some of the events of the past they would realize that what is proposed here now is far from being what they have described, and particularly what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) has called, an attempt at indirect closure. That, of course, is quite absurd. I know that on reflection the hon. member will realize that he was, to put it mildly, only exaggerating for the sake of emphasis, and that if he persisted in that exaggeration he would be using an even more ridiculous argument than even he usually does.
Let us think about what closure is. The hon. member knows what closure is because he was sitting on the government side of the house when the government of which he was a member resorted to closure. Closure, of course, limits the rights of hon. members to speak. There is no limitation on the rights of hon. members to speak under the motion now before the house. All that is being done is that the hours available for debate are being extended.
It is interesting to compare what is being done now with what was done in the past. Because my hon. friend has said there is a complete lack of courtesy and consideration being shown by the government for the opposition, and also because my hon. friend has said that in the past when the party of which he is a member was in power the government always showed what he described as the most extensive consideration for the opposition, let me just remind him of the sort of thing the former administration did when they were in power. I have but to refer to the pipe line debate, when closure was used so brutally and unfeelingly in an attempt to jam through the house a measure on which the government of the day was not prepared to have a full debate.

speechtext: Oh, no.
