subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: I am not in a position to say whether or not there was consultation, or to assess the extent of the conversations to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has referred, but it is apparent that there were conversations regarding this matter of sitting on Saturdays.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: There were none.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: That is all my hon. friends are objecting to. That is the basis of their objection. That was the argument of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: It was not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
It does not matter how reasonable the extension is; now it is on the order paper without consultation so we are going to oppose it. That was the gravamen of his argument.
Let me refer to another example of the former government showing courtesy and consideration as recently as 1956, when Mr. Harris, the then house leader to whom my hon. friend referred in such glowing terms as being the paragon of consideration for the opposition, was endeavouring to close the session. He announced as reported at page 7427 of Hansard-

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: What date was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
August 10, 1956. The hon. gentleman announced on that occasion:
In the past week it had been my understanding that we would wind up tomorrow night. That being the case the following is what will have to be disposed of: labour, citizenship and immigration, legislation, justice, fisheries, post office, public works, C.B.C. and finance.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: That appears to be only a statement of fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: There were nine departments whose estimates were yet to be considered and the house leader of that day said that the session must end the following night.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: He did not say it must.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: He said it was the understanding, so we would have to deal with nine departments.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: You agreed to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: My hon. friend should not be so impatient. On that occasion Mr. Harris announced that the following would have to be disposed of: labour, citizenship and immigration, legislation, justice, fisheries, post office, public works, C.B.C. and finance. And then because a member of the opposition- the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green)-dared to ask in what order that extensive list of nine items would be called, what did the house leader then say? He said: "I will tell you the order-"

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: "-if you will agree that we will finish tomorrow night."

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Read what he said. Never mind your paraphrases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Certainly, Mr. Speaker, I will read what was said:

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: May I ask the minister in what order these estimates will be taken?

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: We will accommodate ourselves to the opposition in that, on the understanding of course that we will finish tomorrow night.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: That is Liberal autocracy. You should not have asked that question, Jack.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: One could cite other examples of attempts by the government which was in office just before we came in to put pressure unmercifully on the opposition, and to bludgeon the opposition into agreeing to end the session on a certain day and on certain conditions. No such attempt is being made here.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Fifty three hours a week.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has said that the session will continue so long as there is business before the house, and that no attempt will be made to cut off debate. What we are asking for now is an extension of the hours so that members may dispose of the business of the house and then may have an opportunity to spend some time with their families. I am sure there are hon. members on both sides of the house who would like to get home, but who realize they should not go home until their parliamentary duty is done. An attempt is being made to enable them to discharge their parliamentary duties and still have some chance to enjoy the summer weather with their families.
Far from being a tactic like that used before, when threats and coercion were resorted to by the former administration to get the house to close the session, this is the very opposite. This is a request for the co-operation of the house to take all the time it wishes, but to take advantage of the time that is available to close this session on a reasonable date.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice seems to receive more applause than the Prime Minister. After listening to the hon. gentleman's remarks I suggest that his party should repeal the word "progressive", because everything they are doing hinges entirely on what the Liberal party did when they were in office. They engage in condemnation of each other.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: On the contrary, what we are doing is quite different from what was done by my hon. friends opposite.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
It is a mutual condemnation society in that regard. I would point out that if the Liberal party persists in changing its mind and attitude every fifteen minutes it is really going to develop schizophrenia. It will be recalled that it was on May 30, I believe, that a motion was first made to extend the hours of sitting, and at that time
Business of the House the Liberal party agreed. They wanted to extend the hours of sitting a few short weeks ago. At that time we moved an amendment which would have altered the proposal somewhat, and the Liberals voted against our suggestion. If the Liberal party had had any courage and intestinal fortitude on May 30 and had advocated the things it is advocating now, such as a summer recess and fall sitting, perhaps we might have obtained them, but instead they chose to be subservient and to agree with everything the government suggested. But they should at least be consistent in their attitude.
I simply wish to say that I for one am opposed to this attempt on the part of the government to legislate by force, compulsion and exhaustion, which is exactly what it is. We cannot possibly give the necessary full consideration to all the items before us when we are sitting practically round the clock. We cannot properly attend to all our duties, and even when we try to we are in many cases doublecrossed by certain other people in the house.
A case in point is the banking and commerce committee. Following the announcement of the Prime Minister that everything would be done so far as committees were concerned to make sure that there was an opportunity for members to discharge their duties fully, an agreement was reached in that committee, which was sitting at the same time as the house, that the committee would not sit when it was necessary for members to attend to matters in the house. Subsequently we found that this was not the case, and certain members were prevented by circumstances from attending the banking and commerce committee and discussing one of the most vital and important matters that has been before the house in quite a number of years, the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act. This was not in keeping with the promise made by the Prime Minister.
This is another example of the attempt to ram legislation through parliament in the shortest possible time, hoping that members will become so exhausted by the number of hours they have to spend dealing with these matters that eventually they will give up and say go ahead; have your way; get rid of parliament so you can run things by order in council. The shades of C. D. Howe are coming right back again, and if this messiah from Prince Albert does not watch out he will be tagged in the same way C. D. Howe was.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the Prime Minister rises I should like to address myself directly to him as Prime Minister and leader of the house. I make an appeal to him in the light of what

Business of the House I think he will recognize are his responsibilities. He has said that he wants to see us discharge our responsibilities, which he recognizes as existing primarily in this chamber as distinguished from the committees of the house. I suggest to the Prime Minister that we should take a look at the work that still remains to be done.
The estimates of 11 departments have yet to be discussed in the house. Among these are national defence, labour, finance and trade and commerce. Is it at all likely that we can discharge our responsibilities, particularly with respect to these four departments, in a one-day discussion for each department? Is it likely that we can finish public works in less than a day? I ask the Prime Minister to look not only at the work that remains to be done with regard to estimates, but also to bear in mind the discussion that must inevitably ensue when the combines bill comes back to the house. That is one of the most important measures that we will consider this session. It is a matter involving important considerations and important differences between the positions taken by the right hon. gentleman and those who support him and those of us who sit on this side of the house.
The bill of rights, now being discussed in the special committee, is a matter to which the Prime Minister attaches great importance, and rightly so. In the light of the submissions already made in that committee, it must inevitably engage the house in considerable discussion when it comes back. In addition, there are now five committees, whose work has not been finished and which are still sitting, agriculture, the special committee on human rights and fundamental freedoms, defence expenditures, private bills and the broadcasting committee. Then there are three committees that are standing by.
In the face of all this it seems to me we have to recognize what is inevitable, unless we are prepared to provide for the dispatch of public business without the kind of care which in conscience all of us feel should be given to these matters. If that is the situation, does it seem at all reasonable to the Prime Minister that we can properly finish our work in anything less than a month? I do not believe we can discharge the work that lies ahead in anything less than three and a half weeks to one month. It may be that if other matters come before the house it will take us longer.
I appreciate the situation in which the Prime Minister finds himself, a situation in which I am sure other prime ministers have found themselves. The Prime Minister is a hard working man and so are the members
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).!

of the government. They would like an opportunity to consider the responsibilities of the government as a whole as well as departmental responsibilities. They would naturally be disposed to be free from parliamentary obligations in order to attend to these concerns.
I do not fail to appreciate that point, but what I am saying to the Prime Minister is this. I am not arguing who is responsible for the present situation, because that argument has been made; but I say to the Prime Minister, does it not seem reasonable that in the face of this situation parliament should now adjourn, come back in the fall and discharge these responsibilities in a manner in keeping with the matters that are before us?
I want to say something about committee work. I am a member of the committee on human rights, a committee to which the Prime Minister said that bill would be referred with the opportunity to give it the fullest study. That committee has been meeting three times a day. I have before me the record of the sittings of the committee. For instance, on Thursday, July 21, it met at
9.30	a.m. and is to meet again at 2 p.m. and 8 p.m. Does the Prime Minister think for one minute that a member of that committee can discharge his obligations in this chamber and at the same time discharge his obligations as a member of that committee?
On Wednesday, July 20, the broadcasting committee met at 9 a.m., the miscellaneous private bills committee considering divorce matters at 10 a.m., the human rights and fundamental freedoms committee at 10 a.m., and the defence expenditures committee at
3.30	p.m., while very important matters were being discussed in the house.
I ask the Prime Minister to consider the situation that confronted us last Thursday and Friday. The Secretary of State for External Affairs introduced his estimates. He made a statement on foreign policy, something which at this time, in this turbulent, troubled world of ours, must be recognized as of great importance to everyone in this house and in this country. The Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke, and though not out of any disregard for him, there were just a handful of members in the house, on both the government and opposition sides. I am sure that no member was shirking his responsibility. Members were in committees. They should have been in this house at that time, listening to the important statement being made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on foreign policy. They had a divided allegiance. I am not suggesting that any hon. member was not discharging his responsibility; I am just pointing out

that the way the committees are meeting simultaneously, three times a day, it is impossible for an hon. member to properly discharge his responsibilities in this chamber.
I had the responsibility of following the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I finished, I think it was, around 12.30 that day. The Leader of the Opposition spoke on the following day between one and two o'clock. Hon. members may not always agree with what the Leader of the Opposition has to say, but all will recognize that he occupies in this house a very important position. Next to the Prime Minister and apart from yourself, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition is the most important official in this house under our practices and under our usages. When the Leader of the Opposition spoke, in spite of the fact that all hon. members would want to listen to him in the light of his great experience, there were but a few members on all sides of the house present.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Why was this so? It was because they were engaged elsewhere in the various committees, one of which was sitting at 1.30.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Would the hon. member tell us how large his audience was?

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: I regret to say to my hon. friend that I would not have as great an audience as he would. I recognize, of course, that when he speaks this house is filled.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: You seem to be worried about the number of people listening to you.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Some day I hope to attain my hon. friend's eminence and have a great audience, but I must be patient and wait until that day arrives. I regret that the Minister of Trade and Commerce should interject because surely, as leader of the government in the house, he should be interested in seeing to it that when important measures are discussed, particularly by the leaders, members are given the opportunity of attending in this chamber.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: I watch for your attendance constantly.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
If the minister watches for my attendance he will find there is no one in this house who is more faithful in his attendance. I am not anxious to engage in any acrimonious debate. I am addressing myself to the Prime Minister, who rightfully regards himself as a House of Commons man. I ask him to consider the
Business of the House situation particularly with regard to committees. I ask him to go back to July 4 and see how committees have been meeting simultaneously during the discussion of important matters in this chamber.
Now, on February 13, 1959-the Leader of the Opposition has referred to this, but I believe it is worth repeating-the Prime Minister used these words, and I am asking the Prime Minister to consider them, to consider them apart from the argument this morning, and to consider them in the light of the desire all of us have to discharge our responsibilities:
We have done everything to ensure that every opportunity will be given to the opposition to discharge its responsibilities in a proper manner.
I ask the Prime Minister to listen to this:
I for one will say unequivocally that if at any time there is any action taken that would deny members of the opposition a fair opportunity of discharging their responsibility, I shall immediately see to it that a change is made in order to assure justice and fairness.
On the basis of that statement I ask the Prime Minister to consider whether that is not the very situation now. Let me tell the Prime Minister that when he was introducing the bill of rights, on July 1, the banking and commerce committee was sitting. I suggested in that committee that since the Prime Minister was going to speak in the house, the duty of every member of that committee was to be in this chamber. All hon. members agreed, and we came in to listen to the Prime Minister, as I think we should have done. The same courtesy was not accorded the Leader of the Opposition on another occasion although I pointed out in committee at the time that the Leader of the Opposition was speaking on foreign affairs and that the members of our party, at any rate, thought we should be in the House of Commons to discharge our responsibility here.
I say this further to the Prime Minister. If a particular committee is going to discharge its responsibilities in the manner in which the Prime Minister said he would see that it was allowed to do, then we should proceed in a more orderly way. I am not saying this by way of criticism of the chairman of committees. We should proceed in a more orderly way in the consideration of the matters referred to the committees. We should give the witnesses who are to be called an opportunity to prepare. Here we have the Canadian Labour Congress asking that the bill of rights be put over because they have not had a chance to give careful consideration to this measure. The Prime Minister and I may have our views as to whether or not
6670	HOUSE OF
Business of the House that is the case. I see him making notes. However, this statement was made by the president of the Canadian Labour Congress. Then Professor Scott, who had been called-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Order. I know the Leader of the Opposition made a statement about what went on within the committees, but it is strictly out of order to discuss the proceedings of a committee which has not reported. I hope the hon. member, in making his point concerning the difficulty with simultaneous committee meetings, will not discuss what goes on in the committee meetings.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
I say to the
Prime Minister that this parliament is criticized. It is said that we are not efficient. Both the Prime Minister and I, as well as other members, are aware of the criticism, much of it exaggerated. I say to the Prime Minister that he, more than any other member in this house, has the opportunity of correcting and dealing with this criticism effectively. I suggest to him that he postpone this motion for two weeks; that he engage in consultation with the leader of the house and others concerning the situation as it will then present itself. I suggest further to the Prime Minister that without imposing his will on any committee, he should discuss the matter with the chairmen of the committees to see if we cannot so arrange our business, even at this late date, to ensure that we can discharge our responsibility without moving from one committee into this house and going back to another committee.
The other night the Minister of National Health and Welfare spoke while I was attending a committee. The minister complained that I was not in the house. I had to come into this chamber, thereby missing the work that had already been undertaken by me and others in the committee. I merely mention these personal references to indicate to the Prime Minister how unsatisfactory the present arrangement is and how, because of it, we will receive from the people at large, all of us in this house-I am not now speaking politically-condemnation for the way in which the public business is being discharged.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: There is nothing new in it; it was done under your regime.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Supposing there is nothing new; supposing in the past-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: How wrong you were then.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Supposing the former administration had been guilty of everything the hon. gentleman says.


Suppose that was the case. I am now speaking directly to the Prime Minister, and I am saying this. Notwithstanding what may have been the situation, I am now asking the Prime Minister to address himself to this particular situation. Let him give the leadership in this matter which I believe it is his duty and responsibility to give. I ask him to remember the words which he uttered on February 25 of this session when, as reported at page 1435 of Hansard, he said this:
I entirely confirm the remarks I made at that time-
He confirmed the remarks made on February 13, 1959 to which I have referred.
-and X would not alter or change any portion of them. However, the important part of my statement was that if at any time hon. gentlemen opposite found themselves in a position of difficulty in endeavouring to perform their duties in committees as well as in the house, no member of a committee would endeavour on such occasions to deny the house the fullest opportunity to enjoy the contributions of those gentlemen who were desirous of speaking in the house.
Those were the words of the Prime Minister.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: You are out of order.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Those were good and wise words. They apply to this situation. I ask the Prime Minister, as the leader of this house, to recall those words and take those initiatives, in consultation with other parties, that will lead to a more orderly arrangement for the discussion of the public business. In that way, more than in any other, the Prime Minister will be able to contribute to breaking down the suggestion that this parliament as presently composed has deteriorated, has become inefficient and has not lived up to the traditions of its predecessors.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: I do not believe that. I share with the Prime Minister the belief that that is not the situation, but he has the opportunity, more than anyone else, to see that that is not the case.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time in order to make a plea not for ourselves, because it does not appear that this matter is of any consequence, but rather to make a plea for the staffs who are concerned with this speed-up with which we are faced. It seems to me that what Canada needs and has needed for some time is not a new government but rather a union for both members of parliament and the staffs of the House of Commons.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: I know of no union that would allow its employees to work beyond the hours that are laid down by statute as law, which would be 48 hours a week. This would apply to members of parliament if we had a union-

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: -and it would also apply to the staff. Hon. members may laugh, Mr. Speaker, because they depend on the Prime Minister to make their decisions and he does not make them. He has intimated that the government do not favour the idea of a 48 hour week for members of parliament, but we do not stop with members of parliament. It is maybe all right for his own political party when he says they can make a decision that they are going to work longer hours, but I do not think it is fair for him to apply that when there are many committees still sitting. However, I am not making this plea for members of parliament. They are quite able to rise in their places and make a plea for themselves. I am making a plea for the staffs of the House of Commons and those people who are dependent on us to speak for them because they do not have a union or have not seen fit to form a union for themselves.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: They will not vote C.C.F.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
It seems to me that at a time when we are working them overtime the least we could do would be to pay them for that overtime. I am thinking of the secretaries who will have to work on Saturdays. We even make it a condition that they must have had a full period of employment, that they have lost no time, before they even get paid for the extra day they will have to work. In the past promises have been made that they would be paid and they have not been paid; and they have no recourse except through requests to yourself, Mr. Speaker, in a personal way. If we had a trade union I suggest they would not be asked to work these extra hours.
I think some consideration should be given to them. I think the Prime Minister should also take into consideration the remarks that have been made not only in this debate but in other debates and that, when he speaks, he should tell the house that he is giving consideration to changing the whole procedure of parliament so we can get down to serious business when we are fresh from our ridings; so we can get down to that type of work at that time rather than continue the procedure that we now follow, so we will not be continually faced at the end of the session with this kind of ballyhoo "Let us rush the whole thing through".
Business of the House
I am ashamed of the Minister of Justice for using an argument in his favour and saying that under previous governments seven, eight or nine departments were presented to the house and he was in agreement that those departments could be passed in two days. I think that is a disgrace. If it is necessary for me personally to be obliged to talk on those matters, it will not be accomplished this session in two or three days. These things are going to get consideration. No arrangement is going to be made by this group to see that discussion is discontinued just to see that some members can go home. We in this group have members who travel as far from their homes as do those in any other party.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: The Prime Minister can solve that problem if he wishes to do so. I think he will find some co-operation from us if he will only agree that he is willing to face this problem so that next year we will not be met with this problem again. Then I think we will come to any agreement he wishes to make in order to solve the problem this year. It is true that we have been in session for a considerable length of time. However, if he is not willing to agree that consideration will be given to changing the procedure next year in order to make it possible to have committees meet early in the session so they are finished with their work long before we are in the dying days of the session, then I think it is going to be extremely difficult to get the support of many of the members for a speedup at this stage of the session.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: I was going to ask the hon. member whether he thought he was not doing a wrong to the Minister of Justice when he suggested that the Minister of Justice was in favour of doing nine departments in one day. He never suggested that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: I am not suggesting that the Minister of Justice was in favour of it. I am just saying that he used this as an argument for a speed-up at the present time. I am not saying that he agreed with it or that he did not agree with it, but in using this as an argument he indicated that the parliament in question was over in two days, so I presumed that was the case. May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
The hon. member had
resumed his seat and had simply risen to answer a question, which I believe he has answered. Is the house ready for the question?

speechtext: One o'clock.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Hon. members call "one o'clock", but the rule adopted was that there would be no recess for lunch on days on which the order was "consideration of estimates". This is such a day, in my view. If hon. members differ with me I shall be glad to hear them.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Perhaps we could get unanimous consent to take one hour for lunch today.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: If the rule has been established that we sit through on this day, I think we should observe that rule.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as always there has been a most interesting discussion on the maintenance of the responsibility and the prestige of parliament. That is all to the good. I am not one of those who believe that regard for parliament is decreasing, although everywhere in the free world since the end of world war II there has been a feeling that parliament, in order to make itself more effective and efficient to discharge its responsibilities, should bring about reformation in its operation and technique.
May I point out to begin with that outside of some statements made by the Leader of the Opposition and voiced by one or two others, there has been no suggestion as to what action might be taken in order to bring about a more effective parliament. The Leader of the Opposition indulged in a series of adjectival ejaculations which he uses on every occasion. He has a certain group of words which apparently have become part and parcel of his being which he uses on every occasion to describe every matter with which he disagrees, until the time has arrived when no one takes any particular notice of his views when they are expressed in such exaggerated language.
Mr. Speaker, there are certain arguments which have been advanced. No one could but be touched by the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East. I listened to him and felt that he was speaking with that sincerity that one would expect from the hon. gentleman, and I must say he made an appeal to which I intend to refer a little later on.
Much has been said about government by exhaustion. Much has been said about the
necessity for parliament-and I speak of parliament in the sense of the House of Commons, not in its proper sense-to be able to attack the problems facing Canada at an earlier date than is possible today under the rules. Under the rules as they exist today the debate on the address covers a period of ten days. Mr. Speaker, during that period of time, unless special action is taken, there is no step which can be taken by the House of Commons in connection with the doing of those things and the passing of that legislation which is necessary. We find ourselves in this position every year. We have the period of ten days on the speech from the throne. In no other legislative assembly similar to ours, to my knowledge, is so much time spent on that subject.
I am not taking the United Kingdom parliament as an example for our parliament, but it is the mother of parliaments and I am going to refer to some of the things which could be done. I think there is no reason why that debate should not be reduced so far as the number of days is concerned. Immediately I suggest that the opposition will say that they are being throttled. We must have agreement in this regard; and giving full consideration to the words uttered today I look forward to support on the part of the Leader of the Opposition for the reduction of the period of time taken today-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: We have already agreed to that in committee.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: You are not up to date.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman says it is already agreed to. To reduce it by two days is not going to make very much difference, although it is a step in the direction I have in mind.
Then we have private members' days, which take up a very considerable period of time during the early days of the session. I know that a rules committee has been sitting and that recommendations will be made. I feel that there should be, and there will be, agreement that at the earliest possible period in the session parliament should come to grips with its legislative program, which it cannot do today. It takes several months before parliament is in a position where it can take its legislative program-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: That is not so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to hon. gentlemen opposite. I listened to some statements made by the Leader of the Opposition, and I do not want to refer to them particularly, but I said not a word. Now allow me to speak without having Hansard plastered

with the kind of interruptions which the hon. gentleman sometimes indulges in, which no one else can hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: The Prime Minister does the same thing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Who changed that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
As a matter of fact it was unusual if there were more than two or three questions. We were discharging our responsibilities. We were not remiss in that regard, but our questions had reference to matters of immediate importance. I am not going to deal with the questions that have been asked in the last two or three sessions, but anyone who looks at some of them fairly and objectively cannot but conclude that the rule as to immediacy and urgency has been in the passing years stretched and expanded.
We had come to the point by 1957-1955, 1956 and 1957-where a half hour a day more would be sometimes taken up by questions. Today our question period lasts 40 minutes or more; it is very seldom less, and sometimes it is considerably more. When you multiply the extra time spent on questions by 129, you have 14 or 17 more days utilized in questions than used to be the case. In other

Business of the House words the session of the House of Commons has been extended by some 14 to 17 days as a result of the major extension in the question period.
There is a field, Mr. Speaker, which I believe deserves the attention of hon. gentlemen everywhere in the house. After all, while many of the questions are interesting, no one can deny that others are not so interesting or so necessary to the efficiency of parliament as should be the case and as was contemplated when provision was made for such questions. If we turn to the United Kingdom, on a couple of days in the week questions are directed to the Prime Minister. I think his question is No. 45 on Wednesdays or Thursdays, and then there are supplementary questions. We have a system whereby giving notice has ceased to be the practice. That is different from the situation in the United Kingdom parliament. In other words they have found as a result of the experience of years that impromptu questions do not lead to that elucidation which the questioner must desire when he asks a question, and that they are generally ineffective in every way.
I go on now to answer the argument about the awfulness of parliament sitting these long hours. I am not going back over the experience of the past; that has been referred to by the Minister of Justice. But before the present chamber was built, after the fire, a great number of debates took place at a time when no provision was made for automatic adjournment. The house sat, not extra hours but for a whole week, broken only by the Sabbath, until its decisions were reached. There was no provision for automatic adjournment, and the result was that the house sat on and on. This happened in 1910 and it happened in 1912. I would remind the hon. member for Vancouver East that those were the days when parliament sat at great length, and those were the days of its glory, according to many. We have departed from that practice. They were exhausting days; they were exhaustive days. Nowadays we have an automatic time of adjournment to prevent anything like that taking place.
Mention is often made of the length of speeches. Well, all of us at one time or another have been offenders in this regard. Some of the speeches made over the years are read. Others are measured. The rule at that time was an unlimited speech, and that continued until very recent years. I was reading recently the debate which took place in connection with the Riel rebellion. The first three or four speakers spoke for four hours or more. Then came the leading member of the opposition and he spoke for five hours, as I recollect it. Sir John Macdonald, replying,

said he hoped he would be able to answer for the government within the limit of four hours.
None of us are sorry that those days are gone, but it was not many years ago when speeches in this house ran to four hours. These were the halcyon days to which my hon. friends sometimes look back. Those were the days of Mr. King. When that right hon. gentleman delivered a four-hour speech it was not regarded as an extraordinary, marathon event. We have got away from that.
Go into the galleries of the British House of Lords. For how long would the house listen to anyone but those who have the responsibility of introducing motions or the leader of the opposition and his outstanding chiefs? How many hon. members of that house would listen to an hour speech? Let me read from a book that gives the picture of the British House of Commons as no other small volume does. I sent for it while this argument was going on for the purpose of bringing it to the attention of parliament. The book is entitled "The Purpose of Parliament" and was written by Quintin Hogg. Speaking about long speeches the author says:
The same tendency is seen in the duration of debates upon which depends, of course, the effective right of individual members to be heard. As the original rule was that any member could initiate business, so it also was that any member could speak on business, and debates could therefore go on almost indefinitely.
There is a legislative chamber in North America where only the personal demands of the individual limit the length of the speeches. I was in that chamber on one occasion where a debate was in progress. The hon. member had spoken for eleven hours. No one would interrupt him. Finally he had to conclude. I think of Mr. Lafortune from the city of Montreal. Speaking from memory I think it was in 1910, 1911 or 1912 that at the end of a twelve hour speech that hon. gentleman said, "I am now coming to the crux of my argument". Those days are no different from today except that we have limited ourselves. I was going to add that in the British House of Commons if anyone speaks at length the chamber empties. Reading again from this book:
The budget debate in 1852 began on December 3 with a five-hour speech by the chancellor. The division was taken at 4 a.m. on Friday, December 17. In a famous foreign affairs debate, Palmerston defended his conduct on the 'Don Pacifico' incident in a five-hour speech which lasted from before sunset one summer's night until after dawn the next morning. It was when riding on the morning after this debate that Peel fell from his horse on Constitution Hill and received fatal injuries.
As I say, I have not had an opportunity of examining this book for a long while, but

I thought these references might give some indication as to what the trend is and what our objectives should be. Referring again to the book:
Nowadays, such deliberation would be treated as intolerable long-windedness. The Speaker begins to show signs of impatience when a private member speaks as long as half an hour-
I hasten to add that the reference is to the Speaker of the British House of Commons I continue:
-and although a budget speech is allowed rather more than a full two hours, the usual time for government or front bench opposition speeches is between 45 minutes and an hour and a quarter. The longest debate (apart from that on the address) is normally one or two days; a three-day debate is not by any means a common event even on a vote of censure.
The British house sits for 200 days. They sit far longer hours than we do and, as I have already pointed out, for most of the year. One hon. member said that parliament should sit all the year round, that the longer it sits the more it will gain in dignity, prestige and a sense of public acclaim. Let me read what Right Hon. Winston Churchill, as he then, was, said in 1931, almost 30 years ago, when he came before the select committee on procedure of the British house. His words are found at page 172 of this book:
If you wish to say what is wrong with parliament-it is that it sits far too long in the year. I would lay down that except in times of war or great national emergency parliament should not sit more than five months with the ordinary short intervals, say, occupying six months of the year.
One cannot help but register amazement over the sudden realization on the part of some hon. members that parliament is becoming retrograde and is not enjoying that degree of public acclaim that it should enjoy. Right Hon. Winston Churchill, as he then was, pointed this out 30 years ago. At the height of world war II when Mr. Churchill was the great tribune of the people and was giving leadership not only to the United Kingdom but to all the free world, speaking in the British House of Commons on November 29, 1944 he said:
Do not suppose that you can strengthen parliament by wearying it, and in keeping it in almost continuous session. If you want to reduce the power of parliament, let it sit every day in the year, one-fifth part filled, and then you will find it will be the laughing stock of the nation, instead of being, as it continues to be, in spite of all the strains of modern life, the citadel as well as the cradle of parliamentary institutions throughout the world-
I believe those words are applicable today. He went on to say:
-almost the only successful instance of a legislative body with plenary powers, elected on a universal suffrage, which is capable of discharging with restraint and with resolution, all the functions of peace and war.
Business of the House
I think we must endeavour to bring about reforms. I welcomed the committee that was set up this year and is operating. I also pay my tribute to the hon. members of that committee for the extent to which, in the few weeks they have been sitting, they have reached that agreement which I believe they have achieved, as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition a moment ago. But there are many things that require to be looked into. Not least among these is the question, how to make parliament more effective.
I hope it will be agreed by the house that the rules committee will be set up at the earliest possible date in the next session and will meet to the end that with your assistance, Mr. Speaker, there will be an agreement on the part of hon. members in all parts of the house that we must bring about great changes in the interests of making parliament more effective. I could quote further from this book, but if I have succeeded in interesting hon. members in reading it I have accomplished what I set out to do in that connection.
It is said that we have all these estimates coming before us. In all the years I have been in parliament I do not recall more than two occasions when anybody ever moved to reduce an estimate, or ever divided the house on it. Hon. members opposite resort to condemnation and then conclude by allowing the item to pass. That is why it has been found sufficient in the United Kingdom to deal with the vast number of estimates in the large amounts that come before that parliament in just over one third of the time that we have taken up to this hour. According to my hon. friends opposite, they have just started. In so far as defence is concerned, we have had a committee on defence and it has sat at great length.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Twenty seven times.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Twenty seven times. I cannot think of any questions that the mind of man opposite could evolve which would add anything to the questioning that went on in the informality of that committee.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: If we could get some answers it would be different.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
I can think of suggestions that can be made, and that is why there should be an opportunity for discussion. I have waited for two years to hear any suggestions, responsible in their nature, on the part of the opposition to meet the problem that faces the free world everywhere on the question of defence. One has only to look over the record of the billions of dollars that have been wasted in the free world, not wasted intentionally but as a result of

Business of the House changed and changing conditions. As soon as many of those things which represent the needs of the moment for defence become effective and operative they achieve disuse and are out of date. I am not going to refer to the expression used, but there is a new technique across the nation on the part of the official opposition. The more challenging the statement and the more irresponsible the allegation, the greater certainly they have in their own minds that what they say will be accepted as a model of statesmanship.
We have heard repetitious statements about uncertainty on the part of the government. Last fall we prepared our legislative program and had it available to a degree-this is not criticism of past governments-that certainly has not been excelled on any past occasion. But how do you get this legislation before parliament with the rules as they are today?

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Put it on the order paper, to start with.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
There is the difficulty, When I brought before the house the necessity of expanding the committee system, there were those who said that we really did not need it. I think the committee system has operated to a degree never before achieved in any parliament of which I have been a member. The government has never failed to allow a committee-I use the word "allow" because I can remember days when committee findings were disallowed-even though overwhelmingly composed of members of the government party, to bring in its criticism and condemnation. I want committees to do that, and I know I speak for my colleagues. Benefit can come to a government, to an administration and to a country only to the extent to which fair and responsible criticism is not denied because of political persuasion.
I listened to the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, and I always come back to him as an authority on parliamentary procedure to which he himself gives entire support at all times. He spoke about the terrible days of the present. In the time I have been in the house I have never known a group to talk more, but he seems to have forgotten that. I do not think the hon. member for Laurier was here at the time closure was imposed; he was on another job at that time. However, giving full cognizance to what he said today, I am sure if he had been here there would have been no closure in the unfair, unjust and totally unjustifiable manner in which it was applied.
Because of that I express the hope that the rules committee will give consideration to removing from the rule book the closure


procedure. I hope the committee will do that, because I can say to hon. gentlemen opposite that after what they did to the rule book and to parliamentary procedure I doubt that there will be another government in the next 50 years that will ever dare to bring in closure as they did.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Afterwards.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: You were as close to the merits of the issue then as you are now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman say?

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: I said you were as close to the merits of the issue then as you are now. You spent 19 days then moving phony motions instead of talking about the merits of the proposal.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breion North and Victoria):
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Look who is talking about phony motions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: In the house?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: In the house, yes.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it happens historically that the house rose in June of 1941, and at that time in 1941 Mr. King was preparing to fly the Atlantic.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: So far as the year is concerned, let me identify it. It was the year in which the Hong Kong report came before this house. I remember so well that Mr. King, on that occasion-

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: That was 1942.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
My recollection was that it was 1941. I was speaking from recollection. The hon. gentleman in all his deliberations, as he prepares his expurgated biography, will I am sure look back on that trip and recall the circumstances.
Then I recall that Mr. St. Laurent, during the heat engendered by a long debate, when he was asked why it was that Canadians were not included in the group of nations in the Berlin occupancy, used certain words in the house. He said why, they were kicked out. Hon. gentlemen opposite speak about changes in Hansard. The words "kicked out" appeared in Hansard next day as "left out". I mention that because in the heat of debate many of us, even hon. gentlemen opposite, as the result of fatigue from long hours utter words which bring about results such as that which are understandable.
Now, sir, when I listen to hon. gentlemen opposite posing as the paragons of parliamentary perfection, then I think we have an example of the kind of political shuttlecock that they have been playing with parliament during the last years. There has been a monotonous repetition of words, without even the benefit of the Leader of the Opposition sometimes changing them and using synonyms rather than repetitious words such as he indulged in again today; words that have no meaning when so often repeated.
So far as this motion is concerned, I want to see the fullest possible discussion. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said there has been consultation. On the other side, the Leader of the Opposition said there has not. The hon. member for Laurier says there has, and that there has been a good spirit of co-operation. The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate says that consultation has fallen down during the past several weeks.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege; I do not believe the Prime Minister would wish to misrepresent me.
Business of the House On the contrary, I said that there had not been co-operation in connection with this motion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Even so, I allow the house to take the different statements, the jarring statements that were made first by the Leader of the Opposition, then by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, and finally in that very touching exhortation by the hon. member for Essex East. He blushes to think of the tribute I pay him.
I simply say this is what is being done, and it is an endeavour to secure the fullest consideration, to give everybody ample time for discussion. May I say again that I realize the situation in so far as the committees are concerned. I have found that within the last few weeks the attendance in committees must have been very reasonable, having regard to the experience and all the circumstances. I see no reason why the house should not accept the motion in the form in which it is drawn. I have always desired to co-operate and on past occasions have gone a long way toward making concessions to the opposition because, after all, we must work together; that is our objective and that is our purpose. However, the kind of speech with which the Leader of the Opposition led off, and the words he used, was not the kind of speech that indicated any desire on his part to bring about any alteration in the motion through discussion.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: The Prime Minister was good enough to say he would answer a question of mine when he concluded. My question is this. If, as I understood the Prime Minister to say, he was sure that closure, after its last use, would not be used again for 20 years-

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: For 50 years.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: -for 50 years-I did not hear it correctly-why then did he make the categorical, unqualified promise to abolish it as soon as he got into office?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: I said it would not be used for 50 years, and that is my estimate of the time when a group similar to those who occupied the treasury benches in 1955 will be back in power.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister now answer my question? Why then did he make the categorical, unqualified promise that closure would be abolished in the first session after he became Prime Minister?

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: No answer.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Would the Prime Minister permit another question? He made reference to some remarks by the hon. member for Timiskaming. Would he also like

Division
to make reference to the remarks concerning the staff which the hon. member mentioned?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
That question is a proper one. It is a very difficult position for the staff, and I agree with that. This situation has existed throughout the years, and no words one could utter would be a proper tribute to those officials for the long hours they serve and the difficulties under which they serve. Mention was made of the Hansard staff. Again, may I say this; that the clarity with which they produce the daily record is not excelled anywhere, and I feel very keenly for the officials. I can only say that that has been one of those things that have always caused me considerable thought throughout the years.
Now, when the hon. gentleman mentions this fact and questions the hours, as well as the sitting on Saturday, and how serious that would be, perhaps the members of the C.C.F. would be interested in knowing that the leader of the only C.C.F. government in Canada moved, on April 6, 1960:
That on Saturday next, and on each Saturday until the end of the session, the assembly shall meet at 10 o'clock a.m. and that, in addition to the regular intermission between 5:30 o'clock p.m. and 7:30 o'clock p.m., there shall be an intermission between 12:30 o'clock p.m. and 2:30 o'clock p.m., the order of business on Saturday to be the same as on Friday.
It was found necessary in the legislature of Saskatchewan to sit on Saturdays. One could also, having the same feelings, express the same attitude to those of the staff who, as a result, have to work longer hours.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
I	declare the motion carried.
Is there anything further under motions?

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order on which I should like some direction from Your Honour. During the currency of the vote one of the hon. members left the house. I want to raise this question for your direction, since it involves the chairman of one of the committees.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
The rule is quite specific. Standing order 12 (2) reads:
When Mr. Speaker is putting a question no member shall enter, walk out of or across the house, or make any noise or disturbance.
The hon. member, whoever it was, was out of order in leaving the house during the vote.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext:
Speaking to the point of
order, Mr. Speaker, perhaps some light can be thrown on the matter when it is realized that when the vote was being taken the chairman of the bill of rights committee was leaving in order to attend a meeting of that committee.

subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who left the house was called to the telephone.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SATURDAY SITTINGS-EXTENSION OF SITTING HOURS ON FRIDAYS
speechtext: If the house does not see fit to impose any discipline, perhaps we might proceed to the next order of business.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR REGULATION OF EXTRAPROVINCIAL TRUCKING
PROVISION FOR REGULATION OF EXTRAPROVINCIAL TRUCKING
speechtext:
for leave to introduce Bill No. C-86, to regulate extraprovincial transport.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to provide for the regulation of the extraprovincial trucking industry in order to obtain the maximum public benefit from a truly competitive enterprise system. The control policy is based upon control of entry into the extraprovincial trucking industry by the licensing of services and the control of tariffs.
This control of licensing and tariffs is to be exercised by a federal regulatory mechanism which is referred to in the bill as a joint control board. This board is constituted, as occasion may require, by members from the transport boards of those provinces which have an interest in an extraprovincial licence application. The joint transport board determines whether a licence shall issue and, if issued, sets the tariff for the service. The board weighs its actions on the scale of public convenience and necessity. Its members, as members of the provincial boards, are experienced in applying the public interest to the practical necessities of the trucking industry. Federal control over and 79951-0-421
Inquiries of the Ministry guidance of the joint control board in the national public interest is provided through regulation by the governor in council.
The bill provides for the repeal of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, which is the present federal regulatory control.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: FOLEYET, ONT.    STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, July 18 the hon. member for Timmins asked me a question in these words:
In view of reports that the local and provincial contributions to the Mountjoy flood relief fund will have been distributed in about one month's time, could the Prime Minister say whether the federal government has reached a decision as to the amount or the basis of the federal contribution to this fund.
Later the hon. member added these words:
Could the Prime Minister ascertain whether any of the federal contribution would go toward repaying or refunding the Red Cross, as has been reported is happening with the local and provincial contributions?
Officials of my office have been in touch with the minister of the Ontario government concerned, and I am informed that the community of Mountjoy has not yet completed its estimate of the damages in the area. When the complete assessment of the loss is made, I understand Hon. Mr. Spooner, Ontario minister of lands and forests, will meet with representatives of the Mountjoy community and will then report his findings to the government of Ontario. At this stage the provincial government will consider further the need of application for special federal assistance.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I presume the hour fixed by the committee was dependent on the normal expectation that the orders of the day would be concluded by one o'clock. I am sure that if the representations the hon. member makes to me were made to the committee they could receive proper attention.

subtopic: REPORTED SITTING OF COMMITTEE DURING ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: The committee met in violation of the rules.

subtopic: REPORTED SITTING OF COMMITTEE DURING ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister not realize that the committee is now sitting?

subtopic: REPORTED SITTING OF COMMITTEE DURING ORDERS OF THE DAY

speechtext: Who kept us here until 2.30?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REPORTED SITTING OF COMMITTEE DURING ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Any direction on my part would certainly not be favourably received by the hon. gentleman or any other hon. member of the house.

subtopic: REPORTED SITTING OF COMMITTEE DURING ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED SITTING OF COMMITTEE DURING ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Oh, take up the rest of the day.

subtopic: REPORTED SITTING OF COMMITTEE DURING ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: -I happen to be a member of the bill of rights committee. We understood that the committee would meet today at 2 p.m. We were later informed that it would be meeting at 2.30 p.m. Although no formal notice was given, that was the word received informally. I am now suggesting it is a violation of the privileges of any hon. member to be denied the opportunity of being in the house while orders of the day are under discussion; that when that is the situation the committee should not meet, and that the Prime Minister, who is the leader of the house, should see to it that is not done.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORTED SITTING OF COMMITTEE DURING ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Order. The last observation, of course, was extraneous to the question of privilege. As hon. members know, it is not the responsibility of the Prime Minister to direct whether or not a committee will meet. It is a matter for the committee itself. I do not think the house has any power or jurisdiction to intervene in a meeting of a committee once it has referred a matter to the committee and constituted it to deal with the business referred to it. Therefore I cannot accept the matter as one affecting the privileges of the house.

subtopic: REPORTED SITTING OF COMMITTEE DURING ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: Let it be noted.

speechtext:
Last year in the estimates there was an amount of $1,250,000 for a proposed public building at Grand' Mere. The minister will recall that I asked question No. 65 which was answered on March 1. According to the answer I received, the reason the project was not carried out during the last fiscal year was that the site had been selected and preliminary plans had been completed when representations were received that the site selected was not acceptable. I was also informed at that time that the problem of an alternative site had only been resolved in the past month.
I find that the date of the answer was March 1, so this would mean that the question of the site was resolved in February. I am wondering why this did not leave sufficient time for the preparation of plans so the item would appear in this year's estimates in the amount of $1,250,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext:
We are very anxious to please the people of Grand'Mere. They have a member of parliament who has been quite assiduous in his efforts to get a better site. I thought we had reached agreement, and gave my word that the building would be erected at the site that we had chosen. Then, lo and behold, within three days I had a delegation from Grand'Mere saying they did not want the federal building erected near the cemetery. This group of prominent men protested, so I temporarily called the whole thing off


until the local citizens could at least arrive at some measure of agreement as to what should be done.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext:
The hon. member for that constituency will probably be back in a few minutes and will have some questions to ask. Last year there was also an amount of $550,000 for a proposed public building for the unemployment insurance commission in Quebec. I asked why this project was not carried out last year. In answer to my question it was stated that it was originally the intention to accommodate in this building the Department of National Health and Welfare in addition to the unemployment insurance commission. It was stated also that national health and welfare is at present housed in a temporary building, and since examination indicated that it was still structurally satisfactory it was decided not to provide accommodation for them in this building. It was not, however, possible to reach a decision in this regard until mid-September of 1959, and there has not been sufficient time since to complete the plans.
I should like to ask the minister where national health is located in Quebec city, and how many square feet of floor space they occupy.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext: We will have that answer for my hon. friend shortly.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext:
I find it strange that this project has been delayed, particularly in Quebec city where there was so much unemployment last year. If I recall the figures, I believe unemployment reached between 17,000 and 18,000. The amount that was put in the estimates was $550,000, which would have taken care of the proposed building for the unemployment insurance commission and national health and welfare. Now this year we have an amount of $500,000 in the estimates. I find it strange that the fact national health and welfare did not find it necessary to move from their location only reduced the estimate by $50,000, and that the department did not proceed with this important project in the city of Quebec, particularly for my good friend the parliamentary secretary to the minister.
If we take into account the cost of a building per square foot, which is something like $10 or $11, this means that national health and welfare would have occupied only 5,000 square feet. I was wondering why the building was postponed. Experience has shown that it is always wise to provide more space in a building than you think you are going to need. We have had that experience in Quebec. We built the post office in Quebec in 1937 or 1938 and some years later it was

found to be too small so we are now building a new one. I was wondering why this building was delayed when there was so much unemployment in Quebec city.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext: The accommodation committee which has been discussing this project was unable to agree for some considerable time as to whether it would be a building for the use of the unemployment insurance commission alone or whether it should house several government departments. The committee has now resolved this problem, and it is to be a building for the unemployment insurance commission only.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext: I raised the question because there seemed to be so little difference between the two estimates, the one last year and the one this year. There is a difference of only $50,000. I cannot understand why the plans for the building were not completed, and I can see no reason for the postponement of the project.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext: In reply to my hon. friend, it was not a question of money; it was a question of the proper disposition of the space.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for the past few years the government has been trying to disperse its buildings to serve certain purposes, especially parking and to relieve the congestion in certain regions. Some buildings have been erected quite a distance from the centre of Ottawa. We have on the Quebec side, in the southern part of the Gatineau in the county of Hull, a number of good sites much closer to the main buildings in Ottawa than those buildings which have been erected at Hog's Back. I should like the minister, when he is called upon to consider sites for new buildings, to think of placing them nearer to the parliament buildings than such buildings are being placed now. When the new bridge is constructed it is going to be very easy to come across to Ottawa.
Somebody told me that some of the employees would rather be on the Ontario side than on the Quebec side. I do not believe this should be taken into consideration, because the employees could live in Ottawa if they wanted to and work on the Quebec side. It would give great satisfaction to the municipalities in that area to receive some revenue from such buildings. We are part of the national capital district, and I think we have a right to our share of the buildings. This plan would ameliorate the building situation on the other side and would help the municipalities that would receive the grants given in lieu of taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext:
I want to thank the hon. member for Hull for this suggestion. It is an
Supply-Public Works excellent one, and we will give it careful consideration when we are considering any new buildings.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext: May I ask the minister if there is a target date for the completion of the federal terminal in Quebec city?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
