maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext: Then how can he explain that figure of 55,000 square feet? The difference in the estimates is only $50,000. Surely it costs more than $1 per square foot for a building. I cannot understand that matter at all. There is some misunderstanding somewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA

speechtext:

When the department prepares estimates I therefore think they are mostly accurate. I would ask the minister to explain why there is a difference of only $50,000 when the department that was supposed to be located there needs
55,000	square feet. That is quite a building, one with 55,000 square feet.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext:
Yes, I have it here somewhere. There were in this case seven bids. I supplied my hon. friend with this information many months ago on an order for return. The low bids on this originally were Grenier with a bid of $15,996, the next two bids were Cloutier and Poulin. The others are not relevant at the moment. Then after a great deal of shopping about, just the day before the bids closed the third lowest bidder changed his bid not by $1,000 or by $500 but by an amount of $995, as a result of which the third lowest bidder became the low bidder. He beat the original low bid by $1. Hence he became the low bidder in an amount of $15,995 as against the original low bid of $15,996.
Because we are anxious that in this system of public tender there should be no skulduggery going on in seeking to ascertain

what other people's bids are and then changing a bid at the last moment in order to get in under the wire by $1, after giving the matter the greatest consideration and even after telegrams and wires from a great many people and representations from my friend the hon. member for Levis, the award of this post office contract was made to the original low bidder, namely Mr. Grenier whose bid was the original low bid and is presently $1 higher than that of the man Poulin, who came in at the last moment with a new bid.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE HOUSING    INQUIRY AS TO INCLUSION IN AGENDA
speechtext:
I find the policy followed by the minister strange in the circumstances, because the minister realizes that this is a practice submitted to the department by the Canadian Construction Association; that any contractor may revise his own tender by telegram if the telegram arrives by three o'clock on the day of the opening of tenders. I would recall that these tenders were called and were opened on December 15, I think it was. I cannot understand why the minister should say that the lowest original bidder was Mr. Grenier, because all the tenders were opened on December 15. Hence at that time Mr. Poulin was the lowest bidder by $1.
The $1 has nothing to do with the matter. It is a question of the principle which was involved. I want to raise another
matter which I think is relevant to this vote -which I sought to raise by way of a private members resolution-and that is the whole matter of providing accommodation for automobiles on parliament hill. The subject does not need perhaps to be over-elaborated at this stage of the session but I think it will be quite clear to all hon. members that with the large increase in the use of automobiles and the limited accommodation of the roadways on parliament hill we have an inordinate number of cars parked on the roadways on the hill every day and all day. Even with this improper use of the roadways, marring as it does the beauty of the site, there is not sufficient central accommodation for those persons who come to do business on the hill either in the centre block, as members of the House of Commons or as employees, or in the east or west blocks. In addition, of course, there is insufficient accommodation available for tourists who come to view the buildings or to watch the ceremonial parades that take place on the lawn each morning during the summer months.
My purpose in putting down a private member's resolution was to try to have an opportunity to put forward what I thought was a solution to this problem. Of course, since private members cannot put down a resolution which would involve the expenditure of money, I had to raise it in a somewhat negative form as a resolution recommending consideration of the elimination of parking on parliament hill. I would think it is elementary that the only effective way of eliminating parking on parliament hill is by providing suitable alternative accommodation.
I think we have come to the stage when we require an extensive parking facility to be provided by the federal authority adjacent to the hill. The layout of the land is such that there are several possible sites available. I am sure the architects and engineers will readily find them. West of the main building and the west block there is a whole area on a lower level where a properly planned 

building could be located in such a way that the top would not be visible from the face of the hill; it would be on the level of the surface of the ground at the main part of the hill. In other words, a structure could be built against the cliff to the west of the buildings.
I want to ask the minister to advise us what consideration has been given to this question and what is the nature of any plans concerning a solution of this problem. I should further like to ask the minister when it is anticipated that a start could be made on such a building if construction were approved.
In this connection I would point out that the present vote for public buildings in the Ottawa area is something like one third lower than it was last year, and I would also draw attention to the very serious problem arising in the construction industry in Ottawa at the present time because of the fact that in Ottawa this year there is very much less construction going on than has been the case during the last number of years. I agree that this is not something that the Minister of Public Works can solve by building public works, and I do not suggest that for one minute. But I do suggest this is a proper consideration for him to bear in mind in arranging the timing of the erection of much needed new public buildings in this area. Unemployment in the construction industry in this area is, regrettably, very high at this time.
There is a good deal more that could be said, I suppose, if one were so minded, by way of illustration of the desecration of the beauty of the hill which arises because of the presence of an unduly large number of cars, but I can perhaps leave that point as one which is self-evident. The hon. member for Edmonton West is very much interested in the subject and I might point out that the time taken to travel by automobile from Wellington street to the parking lot at the end of this hill this morning was just under 20 minutes. That was at eleven o'clock, which is probably a bad time of the day, but it does indicate the congestion on the hill.

speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Ottawa West for his inquiry. This is the relevant time to make it. The hon. gentleman has always taken a great interest in the question of parking on parliament hill. May I answer his last observations first? There are several buildings still under construction in the Ottawa area, and there is a great deal of work to be done on many of them. I might mention the post office building, the national research council building on the Montreal road, the mines and technical surveys building and the telecommunications building. There are other buildings on the perimeter, near Hog's Back, which I do not need to mention at this time. Then again, we hope to call tenders this fall for the health and welfare building, and that will be a major undertaking.
In answer to the hon. member's inquiry about parking on the hill, I am glad to be able to report that our department has studies under way involving two basic schemes, the first of which is the construction of an open parking garage at the foot of Bank street. An alternative proposition is the construction of an underground parking garage on parliament hill off Bank street. The first garage would reach down almost to river level and, as the hon. member has suggested, if such a project were proceeded with it would be just high enough above ground level for the cars to get in, and it would in no way interfere with the view. Then there is a third plan which we are considering, and that is to have a huge underground parking area immediately beneath the front lawn of the parliament buildings. That could be arranged without any final interference with the beauty of the lawn. The trouble is that it would be quite an expensive undertaking.
A preliminary estimate of the cost of the open parking garage would be $1 million, and a preliminary estimate of the cost of an underground parking garage would be $1,350,000. We have not yet estimated the cost of the underground parking beneath the front lawn of the parliament buildings. Our studies are by no means completed, and I would be very happy to have suggestions at any time, privately or in any other way, from any members of the house with regard to this question. I shall be happy to discuss this matter with the hon. member for Ottawa West and I shall be equally glad to discuss it with any other Ottawa members who may be interested. I have already discussed it with the hon. member for Carleton, and I shall be glad to consider any ideas that may be 79951-0-422
Supply-Public Works brought up, because the hon. member for Ottawa West is quite right when he says something must be done to get the cars off parliament hill. The total number of cars presently parking on parliament hill is 432. The proposed capacity of either of the proposed garage facilities would be at least 500.

I thank the minister for his answer. When the minister referred to the figure 432 as the total number of cars parking on parliament hill I believe he intended to refer to the number of parking spaces allotted on parliament hill. Actually the total number of cars parking on parliament hill these days is probably in excess of twice that number. Parking on the face of the hill near Wellington street is three abreast now for a certain short period in the morning and it is mostly double-space parking in other areas of the hill. All I intend to indicate is the difference between the number of spaces allocated for parking and the number of cars that actually do park on the hill. It is a very severe problem. It is becoming so acute we must proceed to find some solution of it.

speechtext: Each of the undertakings would accommodate 500 cars.

He will have to approach this on a much larger scale. It is perhaps unfair to indicate a precise figure in a superficial way like this but it would seem to me that from the data now available a closer figure to what is required would be 1,500.
The minister must bear in mind the number of persons who are demanding space adjacent to the three buildings and who are not being considered at all. He must also bear in mind the question of accommodation for tourists to the hill. I make these observations so that they will be borne in mind when this question is being given further consideration.

I wish to raise two other matters. One has to do with the need for a building in Ottawa that would be available to boards conducting public hearings. I have in mind particularly the unsatisfactory accommodation which has been available in the last few years for the tariff board and which is being replaced by new accommodation that is even more unsatisfactory because it is more limited and has less access to the street. The board is being moved from a very defective and unsuitable building where it has had to hold public hearings to another building which is far too small and does not have an elevator entrance and accommodation sufficient to meet the requirements of the board with regard to hearings.
It has to be borne in mind that there are many hearings where as many as 150 businessmen from all over Canada come to the capital to present their cases before the tariff board. References to the board by the government are of necessity increasing and appeals to the board from rulings of the Department of National Revenue are also increasing as the country grows.
This is only one board that needs additional accommodation for conducting public hearings. The national energy board is confronted with a bad situation. It has no appropriate accommodation for conducting public hearings and carries on under makeshift arrangements whereby it uses the board room of the board of transport commissioners or accommodation available at the bureau of statistics building in the west end of the city.
As time goes on, there will be more and more demands for public board rooms to be made available to various boards, commissions and public bodies holding public hearings. I would ask the minister whether or not the government has given consideration to meeting this problem, and whether or not it is proposed to build such accommodation in the central part of the city.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: This is a problem we are considering. We have to consider the pressing problems of each department as well, and further buildings have to be erected. The Department of Agriculture needs space badly, and so does justice. Of course, national health and welfare is getting a building. My friend has made a very real point to which we have given a great deal of consideration. I can assure him that as and when accommodation is provide it will be in the centre of the city.

There is an urgency about this matter that must be appreciated. The Department of National Revenue, by reason of the nature of developments, plays a very active role in government. It does produce a great volume of income, and it does directly affect the business enterprises of this country. Representatives of these enterprises are brought here to deal with important matters, whether appeals from department of revenue rulings to the tariff board or in connection with direct references to the tariff board, and the decisions arrived at affect the economy of the country very directly. Any impairment of the work of the board making these decisions, as a result of defective accommodation is something that no government would want. This is not a new problem, but it is a problem that has become more acute and is becoming more acute each year as the country grows. I hope the minister will consider not only the problem itself, but the urgency in connection with it.

Whatever the amount might be, there is 50 acres of beautiful parkland going to waste right next to the Ottawa river. In 1939, the then prime minister vetoed the expenditure of $5,000 for the maintenance because the war had commenced. I find there is great interest in this walk.
Seriously speaking, it is a lovely area very close to the parliament buildings, and I think it is a shame that in the capital city of Ottawa, this area should be neglected. I suggest that the minister have a survey made of the situation to see what it actually would cost to restore the walk. I am not suggesting it is necessary to build stone walls in many places and other extensive works. If the stone steps were satisfactory, the rest of the walk could be made safe by shoring along the bank without a lot of these stone walls. As

There seems to be no particular reason for this cleaning, and I wish the minister would explain it. I have done some reading on the subject and I have not been able to discover any mention of the use of lemon juice to remove the patina of old statues. My point is that there seems to be no policy in the north with regard to the maintenance of public buildings.
Apparently there is.

What do you know about it? Go back to Lambton.
In Inuvik, for example, the Department of Northern Affairs are apparently responsible for the maintenance of all public buildings

in that township whereas part of the buildings in Fort Smith are controlled by the Department of Northern Affairs and the rest are controlled by the Department of Public Works. In Yellowknife, buildings are maintained and looked after by the Department of Public Works. Would the minister not consider having one department made responsible for maintaining all the public buildings in the Northwest Territories regardless of which department occupies the building? Why should we need to have different maintenance staff and personnel in the departments of northern affairs, transport, public works and the rest of it? Why not have this work done by one department?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
We have found from experience that it is better to have the dominant department take care of the maintenance in any one town. If, for instance, the Department of Northern Affairs is the dominant department, it is responsible for the maintenance of all the public buildings in that town. In another town, where the Department of Transport is the dominant department it would have the maintenance of all the public buildings. We have found that to be a more efficient system, particularly in those places which are so far apart.
It has been pointed out to me that during the period of transition two departments sometimes do maintenance work in one area in some instances, but we hope to have all that straightened out when the transition period is over. Afterwards, the dominant department is in charge of the maintenance work.

In addition to this question of maintenance there is the question of the allocation of buildings. For instance, if the dominant department in Fort Smith is the department of northern affairs, that department would then be responsible for the allocation of the buildings to the various other departments, so what chance would a post office employee stand of getting a house in Fort Smith? The department of northern affairs is naturally going to look after its own people first.
The same thing is true at Inuvik. I personally think that maintenance, allocation and similar functions should come under the control of the Department of Public Works, and if there was a policy laid down under which the Department of Public Works would allocate houses for use by the post office, the department of northern affairs, the Department of Transport and so on, that would work out a great deal better than this present system of the dominant department in any locality allocating the buildings. A case was

brought before me this year of a postmaster in Fort Smith who could not get a house because the department of northern affairs had given the house to a contractor who was doing some work for them. The house had been loaned to the contractor for the use of his personnel, while the postmaster in the same locality went without housing.

On the other hand, nothing appeared in the Daily Commercial News at the time of the second call for tenders because only three Sherbrooke contractors submitted tenders then. Therefore, the Department of Public Works paid an additional amount of $6,826.60 for this job, and I should like a word of explanation.
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I understand the first tender was cancelled because it was decided that the work should come under the winter works program. We are working on plans at the present time to do that wherever we can, particularly as to inside work. We are going to see that our tender calls go out at a time to provide employment during the winter months when it is so much needed. We are sending to the office at Hog's Back to get the data in connection with the second tender call.
I will let the item go by, but will the minister be kind enough to advise me if the second request for tenders was published in the same way as the first one?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I will find out.

I have a problem I should like to bring to the attention of the minister under this item. Last year a new post office building was opened at Port au Port, Newfoundland. Incidentally, I should like to say it is too bad the plans for the building did not take into account the type of work that has to be done in the building. This is a distributing office and the space provided for mail storage is only about 50 per cent of what is required. I recognize that is a matter for the Post Office Department, but here is the point I wish to bring to the minister's attention.
A number of post office boxes have been placed in the lobby of the building. Obviously such boxes are only convenient to people if they can get their mail at any time of the day or at any reasonable time after the post office is closed. The people who have rented these boxes from the department live some considerable distance away on one side of the post office and work some considerable distance away on the other side. They want to collect their mail on their way home from work in the evening. If they were to leave work at 5.30 in the afternoon it is rather doubtful whether they would be able to get to the post office by six o'clock.
Another factor complicating the whole picture is the fact that the post office is operated on Newfoundland time which, as members well know, is based on the time within the western half of the time zone while Harmon air force base, the United States leased base in that part of Newfoundland, operates on the time within the full time zone which is half an hour slower than Newfoundland time. This means that these people using the post office boxes have half an hour less time in which to get to the post office.

Supply-Public Works
I complained to the post office about this, and asked if they could leave the post office open for another half-hour. They replied that they were unwilling to leave the post office open unless the caretaker was in charge of the building. The caretaker comes under the Minister of Public Works. I am not sure the hours the caretaker is working at the moment. If they were from four to six, perhaps if the hours were changed to five to seven the whole problem could be solved. I wonder if the minister would have a look at this problem so these people who paid money for the rental of post office boxes would get the service for which the boxes were intended.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I would be very happy to do that.

344.	Newfoundland, $5,627,500.

There are two or three points I should like to bring to the attention of the minister in connection with this matter. I should like first to refer to that part of northern Newfoundland which is known as the straits of Belle Isle from Flower's Cove north to Eddies Cove, where there are a number of fishing settlements on behalf of which I have made recommendations to the minister for marine construction. This area is populated by about 2,000 people. They are all fisherfolk. Some of the finest fishermen in the province come from there. Fishing is the only industry in the area. If these fishermen are going to carry on the industry in a manner which will provide them with a living they are going to have to be provided with those things which they are not able to provide for themselves.
In this section of Newfoundland I will agree that the cost of marine construction is a little higher than in other places where nature has been a little kinder. I am thinking

of places such as Poynes Cove, Green Island Cove and Green Island Brook. These are not the only places in this area but I know that all these places cannot be served at once. I would hope that attention could be given to these three places and perhaps the others could be looked after at a later date.
I am not too happy with the type of survey that has been made in this area. It is my belief that a little more attention should be paid to the situation in which these people find themselves. These men who are engaged in the fishery live on a very stormy coast. In order to carry on their trade they must use large boats. These boats are large and heavy and have to be launched every morning and hauled up every evening. The amount of work that goes into trying to protect their gear is sometimes much greater than the amount of work they put into the actual fishing industry. If these people were provided with breakwaters or wharves it would be much easier for them to go about their daily duties. I say again, Mr. Chairman, that I am a little concerned about the cursory type of investigation that is made in these places when recommendations are made for marine construction.
As I said before, I am well aware of the fact that construction in these areas will cost just a little bit more than it will cost in some areas farther south. However, I see no reason why that fact should preclude these people from being given the services to which they are justly entitled. I have submitted these recommendations to the minister and I shall, of course, be submitting them to him again. However, I would suggest that the minister instruct his officials to make a careful survey of what is required.
On a previous occasion I wrote the minister about this matter. He replied promptly and gave me the information and told me what the estimated cost of one of the projects would be. Although it is in northern Newfoundland, I visit this area every year and I have some knowledge of small boats, as has the Minister of Public Works.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: But you do not get seasick.

I know what is required in these places. I would request that the minister instruct his officials who make these surveys to pay just a little bit closer attention to what is required.
May I now leave that section of my constituency and move on to another comparatively large fishing centre on the west coast of Newfoundland known as Parson's Pond. Parson's Pond is a land-locked harbour. The only entrance from inside is by way of the river which flows out and for many years fishermen in that area-and they are all
Supply-Public Works good fishermen-have been able to leave Parson's Pond by the mouth of the river and come back in the same way. We have arrived at the point where the river is beginning to silt and the fishermen are not able to leave the harbour now or get in except at half tide or higher.
I know the minister will recognize immediately the inconvenience to which these people are put when they are obliged to leave their homes and go to the fishing grounds and yet must gauge their time of going by the tide because, if the tide is not half up or higher, they are not able to get away. Again, having once reached the fishing ground they are obliged to gauge their time of return so that they will be able to get in at half tide or higher. What happens during a storm? There is no other place within seven or eight miles. If a storm comes up and they are obliged to get back from the fishing ground, if the tide is low they are not able to get into their own harbour.
I have made recommendations to the minister concerning Parson's Pond. Again he replied promptly to me. I hope that in the estimates for next year some provision will be made for dredging and the building of the necessary breakwaters at Parson's Pond.
Again I recognize the fact that this is not an easy problem to solve, as no doubt the minister has been advised by the officials in Newfoundland. I suspect that if it had been an easy problem to solve it would have been done long ago. I suspect it is one of those problems involving shifting sands and that it will require a good deal of survey work and, I suspect, a fair expenditure of money. However, I think Parson's Pond is a sufficiently important place for that expenditure to be made. I would again earnestly recommend to the minister that this work be undertaken.
I now move along to a third area and I want again, as I did just now, to refer to the Port au Port peninsula. The Port au Port peninsula is a peninsula on the west coast of Newfoundland which juts out into the gulf of St. Lawrence. Again it is not a very easy place in which to carry on marine construction and the building of harbours. However, there are one or two places here where some good work could be done. There has been some correspondence with the minister concerning Port au Port bay. I know that some surveys have been made here but nothing concrete has been decided upon.
I should like to point out that in an area of this type the decision as to whether or not work will be done should not be based upon the number of people in the area in

Supply-Public Works which the construction is going to be built but rather on the number of people in the area which that construction will serve. Right in the small fishing cove where the breakwater may be located there may not be any more that 20 families but this breakwater is going to serve not just those 20 families; it is going to serve 200 families in the area around there. Again I make representations to the minister for further consideration on behalf of the people of Port au Port bay.
Recently a statement was made or a rumour was started that work was going to be done in Port au Port bay this year; in fact, according to that statement, the work should have already been started. However, the minister has advised me that there was no substance to this rumour. On the Port au Port peninsula, Port au Port bay is not the only place where there could be marine construction. Again I would suggest to the minister that a careful survey be made and that some action be taken to provide for these people the wharves and breakwaters which they are undoubtedly unable to provide for themselves.
In conclusion, I should like to make some reference to the work that is being done at Codroy harbour. This is the third year during which work is being done on the breakwater at Codroy harbour. When the minister replies I should like him to let me know whether a contract has been let for the present summer, to whom the contract has been awarded and how the work there is progressing.
I have a complaint with regard to the work that was carried on in Codroy harbour last year. My complaint is this. The contractor came in and brought with him some men from outside. He also employed locally some men to do exactly the same work as that which was being done by the men from the outside. A case in point was that of truck drivers. At one period during this construction truck drivers were working more than eight hours a day or at least the trucks were running for more than eight hours a day. One man would operate the truck for eight hours, he would step out of the truck and another man would step in. What I do not understand about this matter is the fact that the men who belonged to Codroy harbour was paid one wage and the man who was brought in from outside and who was doing exactly the same work was paid another wage. I believe that this is a matter which the minister should look into. Last summer, while I was in St. John's, I took occasion to report this matter to the officials in the local office in Newfoundland but it was so late in the season that nothing

could be done about it then. I would hope that the same situation would not obtain during the present season. I would appreciate, however, some information from the minister with regard to the contract and what is being done during the present summer.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In connection with the dredging at Codroy, Newfoundland, may I say that a contract was entered into on June 10, 1960 granting authority for the dredging at the cost of $314,898, to J. P. Porter Company Limited. As far as the breakwater is concerned, no contract has been awarded.
I am sorry but I did not hear what the minister said.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
No contract has been awarded with regard to the breakwater. The hon. member for Humber-St. George's has an excellent grasp of the problems of his riding. The Port au Port project is still under advanced planning consideration. With regard to Parson's Point we are co-ordinating and collecting information.
In connection with the other three areas mentioned initially, the hon. member appreciates the great problems involved there. There is no ingress or egress by way of roads yet and it is very difficult to make the development which the hon. member requests. But as he knows so well, we cannot do all Newfoundland in one year and our vote this year is up $1,390,300 from a year ago. In other words, we are spending $5,627,500 this year on these developments as opposed to $4,237,200 last year.

I recognize what the minister is saying regarding the expenditure of money, but I should also like to point out that while the increase for Newfoundland this year under harbours and rivers is in the amount of some $1,300,000, the amount of money that is being spent on harbours and rivers outside of St. John's is almost 50 per cent of what it was last year. The figure for last year under harbours and rivers outside of St. John's, according to the estimates, was $3,107,200, while this year the amount to be spent is only $1,770,000. I agree with the minister that it is hard to do all these things and certainly they cannot all be done at the same time; but these are important problems and I would ask the minister to give them his special attention.
May I again refer to Port au Port bay. The minister stated that some survey is being made there and that plans are being considered. Is he able to give me any information as to whether or not a site has been selected?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: No site has been selected but they are still considering the very well known Irish name of Piccadilly. Is that the information you required?
Yes, thank you very much.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Is that a satisfactory site?
Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection

345.	Nova Scotia, $3,036,000.

We now have under consideration a group of items which come under harbours and rivers engineering services. I am seriously concerned about the fact that the total amount available for this group for the development of harbours and rivers is reduced this year by $6,684,300. The item we now have under consideration dealing with the province of Nova Scotia shows a decrease of $2,379,500.
I want to repeat what I said yesterday on the first item, that very serious consideration should be given by the department to construction of the type we now have, namely construction of wharves and the development of harbours to provide facilities for fishermen in order to increase their operations and provide additional shore help. I know the government is concerned with the problem of unemployment, but this is a case where something can be done. This is an opening for the government, with co-operation between the departments of fisheries, labour and public works, to have development which would provide additional employment.
I ask the minister to give this matter very serious consideration. I know that public buildings are needed and they will provide employment during construction, but when a wharf is built or a breakwater is constructed in a fishing community it provides facilities for the fishermen to increase their production.
On this item I have one or two questions I would like the minister to answer. On page 456 of the blue book I notice an amount of $260,000 to complete the breakwater at Port Hood. Could the minister advise the committee what part of the amount voted last year, $280,000, has been spent to date? Also, have tenders been called and contracts awarded for this construction?

Could the minister advise the committee if that was the only time tenders were called, or were tenders called before and then cancelled afterward and, if so, for what reason?
Supply-Public Works

Could the minister inform the committee what was the amount paid to the first contractor, Foundation Maritimes Limited, and why was the contract cancelled after the work had been started?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I will look that up. In the
meantime might I answer the question asked by hon. member for Levis about the staff in Montreal city area only. In the year 195960 the number of personnel in the district architects office was seven, and in 1960-61, nine. In the property and building management office in the year 1959-60 there were 574, and this year there is a decrease in the number employed to 546. In the supervisors and foremen's office, in 1959 there were 26 and there are still 26 employed.

While the minister is getting the answer to my last question, I understood this was a contract for the construction of a breakwater between the island of Port Hood and the mainland. Could the minister also advise the committee if any correspondence has been entered into between his department and the province of Nova Scotia about the construction of a causeway to link the island to the mainland? Because I recall that two or three years ago, previous to the 1958 election, one of the members of the cabinet of the present government in a pre-election speech promised solemnly that if the government were returned a causeway to link Port Hood to the mainland would be constructed by the federal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Yes, there was considerable discussion as to that. However, they dropped the causeway; we did not.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
347.	New Brunswick, $2,187,000.

On this item, again I wish to draw to the attention of the committee that there is a reduction this year of $2,901,000 at a time when such constructions are urgently needed in New Brunswick. Yesterday I referred to three projects in my own constituency of Gloucester. I had in mind the extension of a wharf at Maisonnette, the

Supply-Public Works construction of a new wharf at Lower Cara-quet to replace one which was washed away in a storm in 1958, and the request of the fishermen at Pigeon Hill for the construction of a wharf. speechtext: The matter is under review.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
348.	Quebec, $4,006,300.

I see that this covers the repair of retaining walls at Cap de la Madeleine, St. Jean, St. Laurent and Tracy. Does this mean that the Department of Public Works is ready to provide retaining walls wherever they are needed?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The rule is that a retaining wall is given where the erosion is caused by commercial navigation or a federal structure.
That is a continuation of the same policy which was established by Mr. Winters, I believe.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I think the hon. member is right.

Prior to that, retaining walls were granted where there were navigable waters even though navigation was not the main cause of the erosion. In the light of the minister's reply I have to take notice of the fact that it is only in cases of heavy navigation that the Department of Public Works will contribute to the building of retaining walls. I was always under the impression that the law said "navigable" and not "navigated", and I wonder whether the minister would not agree, since he is a lawyer, to make a new study of this question to see whether the interpretation made by Mr. Winters, who was an engineer and not a lawyer, was the correct one. I am told that the expression is "navigable waters" and not "navigated waters". I should be interested if the minister, having studied this matter, would tell us what he intends to do in the future; whether he intends to accept the law as it is written, or change the wording of the law from "navigable waters" to "navigated waters".

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: One can tell that the hon. member for Hull is also a lawyer. He and I will have to sit down and have a pow-wow on that. It involves the interpretation of the British North America Act and other things.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And smoke a pipe of peace?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I have been puffing hard on that for several days, and I am not smoked out yet. However, I would be very happy to discuss this. I think the policy arrived at by Hon. Mr. Winters, for whom I have great respect, was a very reasonable one in the circumstances, particularly in the light of the constitutional obligation of the dominion as distinct from the provinces.

I raise this question because after this decision was taken by Mr. Winters we went to the provincial government to try to get help in this matter and the attorney general of the provincial government of the province of Quebec-I do not know about any of the other provinces-said this was the responsibility of the federal government because, he said, the law states "navigable waters" and not "navigated waters". So this becomes a problem for the municipal authorities who are not responsible in any way whatsoever and who have to carry the cost of these projects. That is the reason why I am again taking up this matter.
I insisted on my point of view as against that of Mr. Winters, and I shall persist until an understanding is reached at least between the provincial and federal governments on this matter. Since the law says "navigable waters" I believe this is the responsibility of the federal government. I admit some lawyers say that the bed of the river is the responsibility of the provinces, but if the bed has been changed by erosion, then who is responsible for that erosion which has affected the bed of the river which is the property of the provincial government? This is a nice question to study, and that is why I have asked the minister to do so.
I do not expect he will be able to give me a definite answer today, but I do not believe the decision of Mr. Winters was altogether fair when there is such a marked difference in the interpretation of the law as between the two senior levels of government.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not know whether I am in order in discussing this matter at this time, but I presume the vote we are considering now is one which has to do with harbours and rivers engineering services, and also with the dredging activities of the department. My understanding is that the Department of Public Works is responsible for dredging activity in all parts of Canada except those

which fall under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport through the national harbours board. If I am right in that, I take it that the Department of Public Works proceeds in two ways: first, it does the work with its own equipment in certain areas and, second it does the work by means of private contractors in other areas. I should like to know what the policy of the department is for the future. Is it the intention of the Department of Public Works to impinge or enter upon the field of private contracting?
My purpose in asking that, of course, as the minister will know, is that in one region of Canada, on the west coast, it has been decided by the government to build a hopper dredge at considerable cost. I should like to ask a series of questions but first would the minister be good enough to tell me why the department has decided to do this in one area of Canada and if it is the intention to proceed in this fashion in other parts of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend, as he knows the government believes in private enterprise. This department intends to continue to have tenders called for contracts wherever it can. There is no question but that it is preferable in matters of this kind to call tenders. We feel that in the long run it saves money for the Canadian taxpayer. We are not intending to impinge on our practice of having tenders called from private entrepreneurs to complete our contracts.
As the hon. member for Laurier who had great experience with the Department of Transport and also as head of the St. Lawrence seaway knows, there are often situations where private enterprise cannot make the grade. It does not pay them to attempt to make the grade in the first place because they are lacking in the equipment required. I know that the hon. member would not expect me at this time to repeat the arguments I made with respect to the dredge which we are having built for use on the west coast. In fact, I have forgotten most of the details of the arguments I used in previous discussions.
Suffice it to say that the Fraser estuary is a particularly difficult matter. It requires that the channel be kept clear for navigation and special and considerable attention must be devoted to it. As I pointed out on a previous occasion, it also requires special equipment. On a previous occasion in another place we attempted to use private enterprise for doing the type of work required on the Fraser estuary and the company was able to supply satisfactory equipment. Private enterprise is always willing to say, "Yes, we can do it," but
Supply-Public Works as a matter of fact no private company in British Columbia has the proper equipment required to do an adequate job on the Fraser estuary.
By the way, what the government has done in this respect does not represent a change in policy. Because our present dredge is rapidly reaching the time when we will have to dispose of it we have ordered this new dredge to take its place when it is completed. We did so unwillingly particularly this year when we are attempting to balance the budget. We disliked the idea of making such a capital investment or even the initial expenditure required for this year. I can assure my hon. friend there is no change in the government's policy. We do have to do certain dredging ourselves but wherever we can conveniently do so we try to have tenders called so there can be universal bids with the lowest bidder getting the contract.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask a few more questions in this connection. Has the minister not found in so far as that particular area is concerned that it is much cheaper to have the work done by private enterprise than by a government-owned dredge, particularly this one which is being built at considerable cost and as alleged by certain informants is being built in large part with foreign equipment? Is it not a fact that the cost of these dredging operations in the estuary of the Fraser river done by the government's hopper dredge will be more expensive than if they were done by private contractors?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I believe my hon. friend broached similar questions to me when we were debating this matter during the winter months. The answer is this. Here it is a hypothetical question because we cannot obtain a hopper dredge to do the work in the Fraser estuary from any private company because they just do not have the equipment. We need a hopper dredge in the Fraser. We find it is needed. No other equipment is satisfactory. We therefore had to build our own dredge because private enterprise did not have the equipment. As a result of building the dredge we have security and are able to face any storm. We can do the work quickly. Dredging is a constant problem in that area. Although we would have liked to have used private enterprise we could not do so because of the impossibility of gettting the proper equipment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The minister has not answered my question. The information I have is that it is less costly to dredge by private companies than it is by government operation. The minister will remember that the fleet of the Department of Transport many years ago was sold to private enterprise

Supply-Public Works because it was too costly to operate. That sale I believe has proved the point I am trying to make now that when the government decided to give dredging work to private contractors it was much less costly, at least in the area I have in mind, the St. Lawrence.
I do not want to pursue this problem unduly but let me return to a matter that interests me at the moment. As the minister knows, there are four areas in the Fraser river, Buoy 0-6, Steveston cut, Tilbury range and Annieville channel, which are advertised for tenders each year through private bids but the excavation in area 1 and area 2, that is Buoy 0-6 and Steveston cut, are always done by the Department of Public Works hopper dredge. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I do not think I can make a comparison here between the cost of private enterprise and the cost of the government dredging this particular part of the Fraser estuary which in recent years has always been done by the hopper dredge because we have not been able to get a tender inasmuch as private companies do not have the equipment that we require.
In other words, if we could get a tender from them we would be glad to give them the work. As a matter of fact, they are always willing to undertake anything but our experience with one company a short time ago resulted not only in their making an unholy mess of the job they should not have undertaken to do but it resulted in their making a substantial claim against the government for reimbursement for the tremendous loss which they sustained.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have here the tenders that were bid by private enterprise for dredging the four areas.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Excuse me. I do not want to interrupt but to clarify my thinking would the hon. member tell me whether the equipment to be used was a hopper dredge?

done by the hopper dredge that the department now has in operation, not the new one under construction, of course. From the information I have it would appear that the prices of the private contractors were lower.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I guess I failed to make my point clear. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
One of the exigencies is that there is no guarantee there will be no squalls, no rain, no storms. We have to keep the channel clear at all times. Our experience is that the dredges owned by private enterprise on the west coast cannot possibly fulfil this need because as soon as a storm is brewing they have to run for cover. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope the minister will not think I am pressing this unduly.

speechtext:

What leads me to bring this matter to the attention of the minister is the experience we had in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway. That is so in connection with so many other things. That is why the government is as popular as it is, because it has recognized that to be a reality. My friend has expressed the situation very well.
However, with regard to this particular operation, as he knows happens in so many other avenues of life, the time comes when the government has to step in and supply its own equipment. True, it may be more expensive, though not to the degree which my hon. friend has suggested, but still we have to bear the extra expense to get the service,

Naturally, we are delighted, in a year when the department reduces its expenditures by over $6 million in this field, to find they have increased their expenditures so markedly at the lakehead. We are going to receive the benefit this year of well over half the expenditure in Ontario for these items. words, one of the men who has been in there, and who is extremely enthusiastic about this scheme, seems to indicate that it is just a question of cost.
I have a suspicion about this Moosonee project which was suggested in 1959 by Premier Frost. The minister will recall that 1959 was an election year. It does not do to be too skeptical of a successful politician like Mr. Frost, so I think we should follow this Moosonee matter carefully. How soon can the minister give us an estimate of the cost of the project for turning Moosonee on James bay into an ocean port? How soon will we have the data that will enable the government to determine the cost?
I ask these questions, Mr. Chairman, because I would not like the project to disappear until Mr. Frost's next election year. speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that in the mind of Premier Frost this is no vision. He is enthusiastic about it. But when all this information is

gathered-and it is not nearly as complicated as the Prince Edward Island causeway; they have not the same problems at all-we hope to give the matter study during the fall and winter and it should not be too long after that time before there is a report. The survey will greatly assist in determining the potentialities of Moosonee as an ocean port and the study will include a study of the possibility of the transshipping of iron ore from Belcher island and Great Whale river to the port of Moosonee. Premier Frost has tremendous enthusiasm about this matter and feels that it would be a great industrial boom in the future, particularly to the north country.

I know that Premier Frost is so enthusiastic that I believe he stated that if the federal government will not come in, Ontario is almost prepared to go it alone. I appreciate having the statement of the minister. I should just like to have from him the assurance that since this is a joint survey there will be no prejudice to members of this house obtaining information at the same time as the provincial people. We have had examples of the provinces, in a bilateral survey situation, making the announcement when members of this house have not had the information. I point out to the minister that this has happened under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources in connection with their road program where the provincial people had the information and were broadcasting it at a time when it was being denied to us. I should like to remind the minister of that fact.
The other point is that in this story from this enthusiastic surveyor he says this:
Surveys have shown that James bay is open water all winter only 15 miles north of the mouth of Moose river. That means it could be an allweather port, with icebreakers having only 15 miles to break through,-
This speculation about its being a winter port and only 15 miles of icebreaking raises all kinds of spectres. I think the minister knows the quandary that the Department of Transport and its minister are in as far as icebreaking in the gulf of St. Lawrence is concerned. There are some people who are willing to argue that we could have icebreaking on the great lakes and keep shipping open into the lakehead, for example, at least two or three months more a year. I know that this aspect of the survey and the recommendations will create interest in much more than the Moosonee area. If one of the contingencies of going ahead is that you are going to be obliged to have icebreaking to make this an all-weather port, then I think
Supply-Public Works the government will have to keep in mind the problem of the St. Lawrence gulf ports and right up to Montreal and would also have to keep in mind the problems of some of the lake ports that could stand icebreaking for long parts of the year.
This is perhaps getting away ahead of things but I like to anticipate difficulty. Since the government has shown some hesitation about what it is doing in the gulf and the river St. Lawrence in so far as icebreaking is concerned, I thought it was worth while to mention it to the minister now.

I should like to mention briefly three items that affect my riding. One of them is really national in its scope. First of all, I should like to take this opportunity of expressing appreciation on behalf of the people of Nipissing for the degree of co-operation received from the minister, the deputy minister and officials in the engineering branch, for their co-operation in handling an extremely difficult situation this spring and summer arising from the high waters in the French river, lake Nipissing, the Sturgeon river and in fact in the entire area.
Without going into detail, may I say that our problem arises-as it does in so many areas throughout the country-from the fact that during the last 50 years the forests have been stripped away through lumbering operations and the clearing of the land for farming and so on.
Naturally spring run-offs and excessive rainfall are no longer held by the watershed but rush quickly through the rivers and streams into lake Nipissing. To further aggravate the situation we have an understandable problem from the fact that the federal government through its engineering branch controls the outflow from lake Nipissing while the inflow is used and controlled by Ontario hydro, the Ontario department of land and forests, private companies and, in some cases, even farmers. There are three dams which control the outflow from lake Nipissing into the French river and which can handle more water than the French river can take. This complex river system has 17 different water levels which must be taken into consideration when planning the removal of any of the several natural chokes that exists in the French river between lake Nipissing and the Georgian bay.
The officials of the department generously agreed to look into this matter again this year. They came to North Bay and sat down with a group of interested people from French river, lake Nipissing and in fact from the whole watershed area. Method was agreed to there by the co-operation of all parties concerned that alleviated the current flooding

I understand that a survey is going to get under way probably in August of this year. AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was in the process of thanking the minister, and through him his officials, for the efficient and co-operative manner in which they worked with the people of my area and myself during the flooding which was occasioned there earlier this year. I should like to thank the officials for coming to North Bay at the time I suggested and sitting down with the people from North Bay, the lake-shore area, Sturgeon Falls and the whole area generally and working out together a solution to the emergency which existed at that time.
I should also like to thank the minister for the decision to carry out a survey as was requested of the French river system to determine if some of the natural chokes there could be removed. I know the officials are very much aware of the problems. There are 17 different water levels in the French river, and to remove some of these chokes might cause mud flats in some areas. This is a fear which exists and I am sure nothing will be done which would envisage bringing about a situation of that kind. The French river district is very popular, and of course any plans for the future must not interfere with the wildlife and the fish conservation in that area.
At this time I should like to place on record the situation which exists on the Ottawa river, and in particular in the Mat-tawa area. This is a matter about which I have corresponded with the minister and his officials for some time. It is a situation which was created when the Ontario hydro built the dams on the Ottawa river. The operation of the dam at Timiskaming and others farther north by the Department of Public Works gives the department a very serious responsibility in this connection.
At Mattawa and in the immediate area a few miles below Mattawa on the Ottawa river
	.

there are again two natural chokes and also a slide from the Quebec side from the bank which has interfered with the normal flow of water. I was pleased this year when the department agreed to have an official visit the area where some examination was made and I understand they will be revisiting the area during the summer for the purpose of determining whether a solution can be found in this regard.
While we are in the Mattawa area I should like to refer to another matter which I brought to the attention of the minister and that is the government dock there. This is a project which we had approved prior to this government coming into office, and I am glad to say that the minister's predecessor complied with the request at that time and constructed the dock. However, perhaps he would permit me to say that it was a rather conservative dock. It was a little on the small side, and I would hope that now that the dock has to be repaired as a result of the high water in the river earlier this year the department will take this opportunity to make an extension or a more liberal addition to that dock. We have had correspondence with the minister and I hope this will be done very soon.
There is also the matter of the wharf at North Bay for which a substantial amount of money is provided in the estimates this year, for which the people in our area are very grateful. This is an important wharf, growing in importance each year, and if the minister would, I merely want him to confirm the fact that this work will be carried out this fall and winter in an effort to create employment during that particular season of the year. This is my understanding and I know that people in our area would be pleased if the minister would confirm this understanding this evening.
Another matter to which I should like to refer briefly is the matter of interference to navigation occasioned by what I call the misuse of Canadian rivers by certain lumber operators. When I say that I am in no way condemning operators in general; in fact, it is the exception rather than the rule. But this is a very real problem in our area and one which I have mentioned on several occasions in this house, in particular in 1956 when the Navigable Waters Protection Act was amended, and again in 1958. This situation is aggravated by what I call the lack of teeth in the Navigable Waters Protection Act itself, and I think I should outline the problems very briefly. I will refer to what has been done in the past and will suggest what in my opinion is the solution.
The problem is occasioned during the spring drive when lumber operators very often farm

out the job of moving the logs to their mills, and this is particularly true in my own area on the Sturgeon river. It is not my intention to go into detail tonight as I have on other occasions by mentioning the firms involved. Some are most co-operative, some are not. In moving these logs on the river, very often it is done with little or no regard to the people using the river in a normal way for navigation purposes. I refer to people such as tourist operators and boat owners and people in the area generally who use these waters. This has resulted in a very serious loss of business to tourist operators and businessmen generally in our area.
In the past, when these circumstances occurred, the local businessmen and tourist operators would complain to their chamber of commerce or town council who in turn got in touch with the offending firm. Sometimes some co-operation was given, and sometimes not. On many occasions this matter came to the attention of the member of parliament who in turn got in touch with the Department of Public Works and the engineering branch. Officials would visit the area, and by that time perhaps nature, or the feeling that some inquiry was going to be made, would cause the situation to be corrected by the offending firm.
This has been going on for the past 40 years in the area of which I am speaking and it is the result of the lack of teeth in the Navigable Waters Protection Act. This is understandable because that act is divided into two parts. The first part comes under the Department of Public Works. It has to do with projects in or under or connected with navigable waters. Part II is concerned with navigation and the use to which the waters may be put. Very often this leads to confusion, and when people go to the Minister of Transport they are referred to the Minister of Public Works and vice versa.
This has been going on for many years, and in 1958, and prior to that, I suggested that an interdepartmental committee be set up of the officials of the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport to study this very real problem and to suggest, I hoped, a solution. I am pleased to say that this committee was set up following my request, and I am also pleased to note that last year, I think it was on June 18, they met in the town of Sturgeon Falls with members of the town council, the chamber of commerce, boat operators and tourist camp operators, and I think some very interesting information was put on the record at that time.
But what has happened since? I should like the minister to comment on the activities of this committee and if possible to tell us
Supply-Public Works what are the government's intentions in this regard. In my words now I am not complaining about the lack of activity on the part of this committee. This committee did go to Sturgeon Falls and meet the people there, but officials of the department cannot move without direction, and I would hope that between the two ministries concerned consultations can be held at the top level in the hope of reaching some satisfactory solution. Either some teeth should be put into the Navigable Waters Act by amending it, or it should be scrapped and this entire responsibility placed with the Department of Transport.

354. Remedial works where damages are caused by, or endanger, navigation, or federal government structures: and the completion of protection works already under way, $700,000.

My first words here tonight will be to extend my sincere gratitude to the Minister of Public Works for the interest he has always evidenced whenever I have brought problems to his attention and also, through him, to extend my gratitude on behalf of my constituents to the departmental officials who have always shown me wonderful co-operation.

Supply-Public Works
In so doing they have given birth to a lot of new structures. They have added that little something to structures which were not as satisfactory as they should have been and in the ultimate an adequacy to the whole that has been very beneficial to the fishermen throughout my constituency. I should like to add my commendation for the institution of rock ballast as a wave breaker throughout the riding of Shelburne-Yar-mouth-Clare.
As hon. members know, we are from a province that is known as the ocean's proud playground that juts out into the Atlantic and therefore is subject to the onslaught of the ocean at its worst. Heavy seas roll in whenever we have storms. A lot of these breakwaters at which in the past could not safely moor fishing boats are now made safe for the mooring of these craft.
The dredging program has been one to which the Department of Public Works has devoted a great deal of interest and cooperation. Breakwaters that in the past were commonly known as highwater passages are now navigable at low tides. I do not have sufficient words at my command to express the gratitude of the people who have to make use of these breakwaters. I sincerely hope that this program will be continued in the years to come.
If I may be permitted to do so I should like to make a suggestion concerning what I might call secondary protection to some of the breakwaters that are located throughout my area. As some hon. members will know there are two varieties of damaging seas, one that comes from a ground swell and the other that derives from a choppy sea. The location of the breakwater governs whether the threat exists on the western or eastern shore and the threat is entirely dependent on the direction of the wind. We have rock talus that prevents the ground swell but in most cases the wharves are left wide open to the northeast wind that kicks up a tremendous choppy sea and can do considerable damage to any of the boats moored at these breakwaters. There may be as many as 20 or 30 boats moored at the same time. It can readily be appreciated that in the event of a northeast gale in certain areas the protection is not as adequate as it should be.
As a remedial suggestion may I suggest that piling be driven at specific intervals. I leave the spacing of the piling to the discretion of the engineers. Planking should be added to low water mark so that when the tide rises in the event of these gales the boats will be fully protected. They are not safe today in the event of a shift of wind, these shifts being prevalent in our part of Nova Scotia. The


danger is particularly great if the crisis occurs when people are sleeping. These could be made absolutely safe at small cost to the department and the government.
I have presented bouquets of thanks to the minister and his departmental officials but I feel I would be remiss in my duty and not fully representing the interests of the people of the Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare constituency if I were not to pluck one little petal and offer it to an hon. member who I see is not in his seat this evening. I refer to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He deserves this tribute for the interest he evinced the other day in the Yarmouth public wharf, a project that has been in the minds of the people there since confederation and which thanks to the alertness of this government has now reached the planning stage. I am happy to say that a site has been purchased and following the announcement made in this chamber 45,000 cubic yards of fill have been removed from the site itself.
Perhaps I may be permitted to advance another suggestion concerning contracts and their award. Throughout my period of time in the House of Commons I have observed that contracts are sometimes late in being awarded. This causes considerable inconvenience to the contractors and to the fishermen as well. Perhaps I may offer a word in clarification of this.
As some hon. members may be aware the height of the lobster fishing season in my part of Nova Scotia, which is district No. 4, begins on December 1 and ends on June 1. Through personal experience I have found that some of these contracts are awarded late in the summer or early in the fall. As I say this is a matter of great inconvenience. The contractor moves in. Sometimes he has to motor 20 miles from the mainland transporting his equipment only to find that the gales that are so prevalent in the fall season prevent him from doing the work he should do. Should the weather by a freak of nature be different from what it ordinarily is, he commences his work. Nevertheless this presents a great deal of inconvenience to the fishermen who wish to start operations on December 1. That period of the year might be described as the klondike season for the autumn lobster fishermen. I would therefore suggest that if it is possible the Department of Public Works should make every possible effort to award contracts early in the month of June so that the projects will be well under way when the lobster season arrives.

358. Maintenance and operation of graving docks, locks and dams, $914,270.

There is one matter that I should like to raise in connection with this item. It has to do with the maintenance of dams. The public works department maintains a number of dams on the Ottawa river in addition to the dams maintained by the Ontario hydro, by private authorities and by the Quebec hydro authorities. The consequence of this has been that the natural flow of the river has been sharply interfered with but that in itself would not be a material consequence were it not for the fact that at the time of the spring run-off there is a great deal of damage being caused along this river through the lack of co-ordination in the operation of the dams.
The main difficulty arises as a result of the failure to open the dams at the appropriate time to release the water held in reserve in advance of the flood waters coming from the upper part of the river. While I have no criticism of the operation of the public works dams in this connection, I want to point out that it is small satisfaction to those riparian owners along the river whose properties are severely damaged by the flood waters to know that the public works department may not be at fault, if through lack of co-ordination the other dams fail to open or close at the appropriate time. The main offender seems to be the Ontario hydro. They seem to persist in ignoring the information as to flood conditions in the river and the timing of the arrival of

the flood waters at the relevant points in so far as the opening and closing of their dams is concerned.
As nearly as I can find out, the system followed by Ontario hydro is that the engineers at the dam projects have no control over the situation at all. They can only open or close the dam on instructions from the head engineers in Toronto, and the head engineers in Toronto either do not receive or refuse to act upon the relevant information as to water conditions in the river. The amount of unnecessary damage caused each year as a result is very great, and it is particularly irritating when it is known that it is not due to flood conditions in the ordinary sense but due to the failure of the authorities operating dams on the river to observe sensible practices.
Bearing that in mind, and bearing in mind that the federal government has jurisdiction over this river because it forms part of the interprovincial boundary and because it is a navigable stream, I am going to propose to the minister something I have proposed unsuccessfully for some years. I suggest that he take the initiative in seeking to obtain proper coordination of the authorities operating all the dams on the river, and that the co-ordinating control be under the jurisdiction of the federal government. I have sufficient confidence in his department to believe that they are capable of exercising that authority in the best interests of all concerned. It is something that is very badly needed.
