I believe you will find item (S) comes under the heading of trans-Canada highway and I should like to mention it at this time. I should just like to bring to the minister's attention the necessity of the completion of the trans-Canada highway. This matter has been of a great deal of interest in Kootenay East for a very great number of years. I can go back to about 1948 when we in the chambers of commerce took an active interest in the completion of this highway. At that time we made several recommendations to the government with regard to our opinions as to where the trans-Canada highway should be developed and also the route at that time.
It is our opinion that the completion of the southern trans-provincial highway No. 3 should receive top priority by the government. This route we feel is most important to all of British Columbia. It is the only all-weather highway we will have in British Columbia going across the complete distance of the province. It is the most important highway connected with the coastal area. At the same time it goes through a highly industrialized section and also the most populated section of the province. It also connects up with all of the United States routes coming from Mexico and California. I also mention route No. 93 which is the only route travelling from Mexico City clean up to Alaska, and connecting up with this southern trans-Canada route.
We understand from press releases that the provincial government have under consideration the construction of a highway from central British Columbia terminating near Jasper, Alberta. We are in favour of this route and we also would support it. But we feel that we cannot support such a program in the north until such time as the more populated industrialized and agricultural areas of British Columbia are being serviced and especially with the trans-Canada highway so that the population and the tourists travelling in Canada can go across our country without having to divert in many cases across the line to the United States and other areas in order to cross a portion of British Columbia.
Another problem that has arisen is the connecting link with the trans-Canada highway. We have a connecting link from the southern route on the trans-Canada highway from Golden which will eventually connect up with the now partially completed highway. As I mentioned, this highway has been under construction a number of years and we feel that the southern route can be built in a

very short time and with very little expense and I would ask the minister's consideration at this time. Also I should like to bring to the minister's attention another thing on which I believe I have the support of the hon. member for Lethbridge, the hon. member for MacLeod, and the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary. I feel that with the concerted effort of all members from British Columbia, especially those from the southern section of the province, we should be able to bring a little bit of pressure upon the Minister of Public Works so that we can get this road completed in the near future.

I find myself in the position of having to support all the proposals put forward by members of the Progressive Conservative party with respect to No. 3 southern trans-provincial highway in British Columbia being the second portion of the second trans-Canada highway. You will note, Mr. Chairman, that when it comes to the matter of the necessities of the Kootenays we stand together on these matters. Of course, we differ as to the route we shall take to accomplish our objectives. But on this occasion the hon. member for Kootenay East has stated the case very well. I am not going to take up the time of the committee to repeat it. I simply want to say "amen" to all he has said during the last few minutes, and I confine myself to those few minutes. I trust the minister will give favourable consideration to his representations, supported by the hon. member for Kootenay West.
There is a big decrease here of $4 million. Does that mean that the amount of $9 million for this year will complete the trans-Canada highway through the national parks?

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to delay the committee at this time with the situation facing us at the moment, and I do not wish to make any criticism. I have only praise for the minister and his department but in connection with the trans-Canada highway 1 am sure there should be strong and definite consideration given to at least an alternate route from Alberta to the west coast.
We all know that the designated route goes through an extremely hazardous area across the Rocky mountains. A recognized alternate route for such an important thing for Canada as a completed trans-Canada highway is just good business. The province of Alberta has on its own brought its highway standards up to the trans-Canada standard for its portion of a second alternate route, namely highway No. 3 from Medicine Hat, through Lethbridge and the Crowsnest
Supply-Public Works pass. With a small amount of work in British Columbia which might be hastened by consideration of this problem by the federal government we could be assured of a reasonable route to the west coast at all times which would be something that Canadian citizens have never before been able to enjoy by way of a Canadian route.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
As I said in the announcement I made on Monday last, it is impossible to estimate that. I tried to get our experts to make an estimate of what is involved here, but as the hon. member appreciates that information is rather difficult to obtain. In the first place we have to see how this proposition of a pre-sold house is going to work *with the builders. You can appreciate that because there is a softness in the market in certain areas, to do what we have done in previous winters, that is, grant a certain number of loans, say 25, to each builder to do speculative building, would be to upset the economy in connection with the areas Where there is a softness in housing.


So because of this new plan which we have, a plan with which we have not had any previous experience to determine how it might affect the number of starts, I would not like to make a guess. I feel just the same way as I think does the hon. member for Levis; I cannot conjecture on the cost of the Northumberland causeway, and I cannot conjecture on the number of starts. But we do know this, and it should cause great satisfaction to the Canadian people, that we will have just as many extra starts as there is demand for housing of this particular category.
I think the hon. member will agree that we have extended the limits and lifted the restrictions on income just as much as we can, and to raise the income limits higher would be only to encourage people to get direct loans from the government who could readily afford to go to the conventional lenders and get their loans there.

It seems inconceivable that the government is embarking on a policy not knowing what results to anticipate. However, it seems to me that the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing must surely know the number of starts that will likely result from this three-month program.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I know the hon. member is an authority on housing, and I always appreciate his assistance as well as his criticism. It is always done in a good natured way. But I can assure him, and I know he will accept my words, that this wonderful organization from which I am accepting advice cannot make any estimate of the number of extra starts. However, I can tell the hon. member that it will be more than 125,000 starts this year and that is what he is really interested in.
May I also tell him I did not realize he was denouncing this new policy the other day. He does it in such a cool and pleasant way that I thought he was really complimenting us on this new policy. It seems the hon. member was really giving us a blast. I was surprised to hear that criticism coming from him. I would have thought he would have been delighted with this new program. There is nothing especially new about this winter program. In 1957, 1958 and 1959 we had a winter program. The hon. member talks about a change in policy. There has been no change in policy as far as a winter program is concerned. I said in the spring that if we could get through without a winter program we would be glad to do so, but there has been here, as in the United States, a definite cutback in housing and therefore we feel it is necessary again to have a winter works program, first, to make more houses available

for our people and, second, and very important, to provide winter work for those in the construction industry who need jobs at this time.
Where is the real criticism? If the hon. member is trying to make political capital out of it, that is fine. I do not mind that. But is there any real criticism of what we are endeavouring to do? In all my remarks I said our future actions would be guided by our experience, and our experience indicates that we need a winter works program in the realm of housing and we are trying to do it in as fair a manner as possible; in a manner which cannot possibly lead to flooding the market with houses that cannot be sold or adding new houses to a market which in some areas, is already soft.

The minister has raised this matter of winter construction. May I take this opportunity of saying that we are very much in favour of a high level of house building in the fall and winter months. There is no doubt about that. However, what is to be gained employment-wise if this results in a decline of jobs in the summer? There is no better example than the events of the past year. Last year we reached a peak in April; this year we have not reached a peak as yet, and if we are only shifting normal summer construction into the winter months I suggest we are not gaining very much. If the government is genuinely concerned, as I am sure it is, to create more jobs in the winter, it seems to me it should offer some form of concession which would encourage construction in this field in the wintertime.
I should like to ask the minister this question. Of the $175 million that he announced earlier this year will be made available, how much has been lent to date? I am not concerned at the moment about how much is being applied for, though that figure would be interesting. I am interested more in how much has been lent up to now.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, I would like briefly to submit to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) a few suggestions with regard to the activities of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporaiton.
First of all, I want to congratulate the minister for easing up credits for housing purposes, which will enable more families of average income to get mortgage loans from the corporation, and also for making direct loans available to contractors, while encouraging them to attract buyers. Such action will also help reduce undue speculation accordingly.
Mr. Chairman, though the housing situation has improved since the end of the last war, we certainly cannot ignore the problem. At least a third of Canadian families have not enough income to buy a new house. At least half a million of those families lack accommodation that could be described as satisfactory. Many existing housing units have reached the critical age limit and, by 1980, at least one million Canadian homes will have reached the age of 75 and over, while a further million will be 50 to 75 years old.
Before long, a new generation, born of marriages that took place in the 40's and which is now crowding schoolrooms, will marry in its turn and seek separate accommodation. According to the estimates of the Gordon commission, the number of housing units should almost double throughout the country from 1955 to 1980.
Such prospects are cause for worry, all the more so because such increases mainly occur in urban communities, and that is why I would suggest to the minister that specialized studies be made without delay from a social and economic point of view, in order to set up a housing program that would adequately provide for new requirements, while taking into consideration the demands of modern town planning.
As a result of this situation, Mr. Chairman, we must pay more and more attention to the redevelopment of slums in our cities where dwellings are becoming unsanitary.

Supply-Public Works
Social problems in addition to the deterioration of buildings are making those areas increasingly costly for taxpayers.
Moreover, and this is another problem I wish to draw to the minister's attention, at the present time wage earners with incomes of only about $3,000 per year-and there are very many of them in Canada-have to give up the idea of owning their own homes, because they cannot make the required down payment and then pay the difference between the total cost and the loan granted. Just the same those less fortunate citizens are entitled and anxious to improve their housing conditions.
In this regard, it is interesting to note the system of co-operative apartments suggested by the Montreal real estate board. The latter suggests, as a means of clearing slums and particularly of settling the housing problem, a program for the construction of cooperative apartments in the centre of the town, where a family might own an apartment in a multi-apartment building rather than always rent or be forced to move to the suburbs, some 15 to 20 miles from their work.
The system has been in use for a number of years in Europe, particularly in France, and was recently introduced in the United States, especially in New York. There is no reason why Canadians should not avail themselves of that solution.
In a co-operative building an apartment can be bought just like a house. You buy an apartment instead of a house, and after a down payment of a few thousands dollars, you can pay the balance at so much per month, with a mortgage as collateral.
Special arrangements are made to spread out over a number of years, and on an equitable basis between the owners-lessees of the apartment building such items as taxes and the cost of repairs to the roof and stairways etc.
Use might be made of the National Housing Act to purchase sites, clear the slums and then build co-operative apartments of that type.
This would enable private enterprise to share in slum clearance and in the construction of living accommodation at very low cost.
To promote this sort of development, the American law allows a shareholder tenant in those co-operative apartments, or in every home built on a co-operative basis to deduct
[Mr. Campeau.l

from his gross income for income tax purposes, the amounts paid during the year to a co-operative housing corporation, as a contribution to taxes or interest on the principal paid by the said corporation. The deductible amount should correspond to the share of the tenant owner and represent his quota of real estate taxes and interest on the principal paid for the acquisition, construction, repair or maintenance of co-operative homes or dwelling units.
Because of the growing success of the cooperative housing movement, it would certainly be appropriate to think of applying the American formula in Canada and thus help hundreds and thousands of Canadians who earn about $3,000 a year to acquire property. The co-operative apartment formula offers an interesting combination to be developed between the rental system and ownership.
The American formula, improved and adapted to our needs perhaps offers the only possible solution of the problem that faces a great number of our citizens who have not the required income to acquire an individual home, but have enough to become tenant-owners. I therefore suggest to the Minister of Public Works to give serious consideration to this solution which is ignored in our National Housing Act.
There is another issue, that of cleaning up the slums that corrode the heart of our cities and towns, and replacing them by sanitary low rental housing units suitable for low income families who are physically and morally rotting in those hovels.
The idea is to find a means of persuading and helping the municipalities to avail themselves fully of the National Housing Act.
Such a measure would have the effect of opening up a new market for construction in urban centres at a time when construction is slow. It must not be forgotten that industrial production is more and more dependent on construction, which is the most seasonal of industries. It is therefore necessary to insure a certain stability to the building industry by methods designed to strengthen the value of the tremendous investments now existing in Canadian cities.
In Montreal, the municipal authorities recently initiated an urban renewal program covering the whole of the municipal territory. The carrying out of the operation will be directed by a housing and renovation committee of which one of the most active members-it gives me pleasure to mention the

fact-is one of my colleagues on the other side of the house, the hon. member for St. Ann (Mr. Loiselle).
This committee, whose members work hard and have done a tremendous task in a short time, has found that there are 23,000 housing units in Montreal whose construction dates back at least to 1871; that 25,000 units are in need of major repairs and that 25,000 units are either defective or blighted. In those slum areas, there is a higher rate of crime, delinquency and sickness, not to mention the loss of tax revenues caused to the city by the drop in real estate values.
A preliminary survey carried out on behalf of the city of Montreal by the Montreal economic research corporation shows there are 50 zones subject to renewal, of which 12 should be cleared of slums to make room for low rental housing projects, 16 would require to be cleared of their slums and rehabilitated, and 22 should be cleared of slums and used for industrial and business purposes.
This renewal program, apart from providing an adequate solution to the problem of sanitary housing, will help carry out great town planning schemes such as a projected throughway along the harbour, the widening of streets, parking accommodation, the radio and television centre and the administrative centre in the eastern part of the city.
Montreal authorities have already started three great surveys to put this total program under way. First, a general survey will be conducted on urban renewal for the entire city territory, covering about 120,000 buildings of which half are blighted, in order to determine the location of slum and low grade housing areas. That survey will allow the development of a program whose implementation would be carried out according to the priority of importance or urgency of the projects. Second, a renovation survey for the eastern part of the centre of the city covering about 10,000 buildings and 25,000 families, to obtain the essential details for the development of specific slum clearing and reconstruction projects including a radio and television centre, a civic centre, as I said a moment ago, as well as low rental housing. Third, a low rental housing project in the St. Sulpice domaine, a vast area of more than 300 acres, which the municipal authorities have had the wisdom of buying in the past. It is the intention of the city of Montreal to promote there, in addition to low 79951-0-424J
Supply-Public Works rental housing, the construction of family housing, through co-operative projects.
The city of Montreal has submitted two requests to the Department of Public Works in order to obtain a subsidy in the case of the first two surveys and will submit another one shortly for the third one.
In view of the importance and urgency of those surveys, and in view of the unemployment relief works which they are bound to bring about in a near future, I hope and trust that the Minister of Public Works will see to it that those requests for subsidies are promptly processed and granted without delay.
Those slum clearing projects, in the eastern part of the city, have been approved by the commercial centre of Montreal-whose development committee is presided over with a remarkable civic spirit, by Mr. Gabriel Gre-goire-and by all civic and commercial organizations. They obviously got the approval of authorities concerned, the provincial government, the C.B.C. and the city council, where approval was granted unanimously.
The building of a television and radio centre in the "Quebec suburbs" will bring about the redevelopment of a district doomed to decay because up to now no government took interest in its rehabilitation.
Those measures are only the beginning of a large scale works project in the very centre of Montreal. It is up to the C.M.H.C. to pursue the policy of understanding and action it has always applied up to now in the city of Montreal.
I take this opportunity to thank the officials of the corporation and in particular Messrs. Bates, Sicard, Marier, Cole, Hignett, Armstrong, St. Pierre and many others and to congratulate them on the good citizenship they showed in the discharge of their duties. I am sure that the Minister of Public Works who has always shown interest in

Supply-Public Works Montreal will see to it that the federal government take proper action without delay.

I want to raise two particular matters with the minister. I am bothered, first of all, by the mortgage insurance fund that Central Mortgage and Housing is building up. If the minister checks on page 809 of Hansard, he will find that Central Mortgage and Housing made a return in answer to a question which indicated that since January 1, 1957 to January 1, 1960, that is a three-year period, this mortgage insurance fund had increased from $22 million to $61 million. The contingent insurance liability on insured loans and section 40 loans, that is I take it what the fund is covering, has increased from about $1,100 million to $2,357 million. In other words, the actual mortgage fund must be increasing faster than the liability against it.
Since the information also filed on page 861 of Hansard, in addition to that on page 809, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska, indicates that since 1954 Central Mortgage and Housing has had remarkably few properties returned to them by default, it would seem that the rate of percentage which is set to feed money into the mortgage fund is too high. I should like an explanation from the minister as to why it is not possible to lower the percentage insurance charge to those who borrow from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. When 1 brought this matter up in a more tentative way with the former minister of public works on these estimates he told me that this build-up in the fund was needed because of the large liability and the possible collapse in Elliot Lake.
Elliot Lake is the most delicate situation involved in this mortgage insurance fund. I should like to hear from the minister the number of units in Elliot Lake that are covered by this mortgage insurance fund. 1 should like to know the total liability in dollars on those units. 1 should like to have from him some indication of the number of houses that have come back by default to the government in the Elliot Lake area in the first six months of 1960. Unless there is a very strong indication that the Elliot Lake situation is going to place an inordinate drain upon this mortgage insurance fund, I would suggest to the minister that the statistical table indicates the insurance rate is too high. I am sure that the fund must have over $70 million in it now.

Unless the Elliot Lake situation is proving that this fund is going to have an inordinate demand upon it, I would suggest the government should give serious consideration to reducing the insurance rate. I should like to know also from the minister what is being done with this money. Where is it invested, and at what rate of interest? Since the information that was filed in February would indicate a remarkably small number of claims against the fund, a remarkably low number of loans in default, I really would urge him to consider reducing this particular percentage. It seems to me that government operations tend to become quite inflexible. But surely the experience of just these three years would seem to indicate that this fund is piling up at a greater rate than is needed.
The second point I want to bring to the minister's attention also relates to some information filed in the house in answer to a question on June 15, 1960. This is in connection with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation low cost minimum house design. The minister may remember that the former minister announced this design with a great flourish in October of 1958. This was one of the first measures the minister brought in after that great election victory and he made it appear as though this attempt by C.M.H.C., with this design 2000, was going to bring in possibilities for many people in rural areas and small towns and with low incomes to take advantage of the mortgage funds that had been going to people with higher incomes and in metropolitan areas. Now we have the results filed here for the first 16 months that these designs were available, and I think the minister will agree that the total number of units of these small designs, either design 2000 or designs with less than 900 square feet, of 1,829 in 16 months is rather low. For example, in Newfoundland I would imagine the need is great for this kind of housing. However, only five units were built there. In Ontario, which is the greatest of the provinces in terms of population, only 501 units were built. The average estimated cost was $9,200. A $9,200 house or new home is a low cost home in Ontario today. But I am sure the minister and his officials would agree that there is a much greater demand than this response would indicate.
I should like from him an explanation as to why these low cost designs have not caught on and what steps C.M.H.C. is considering in order to get more homes built in this particular price range. If the minister looks at the total number of units, namely 1,829, and relates it to the figure of which he is so proud,

namely 125,000 or 140,000 starts in a comparable period, he can see that it is slightly over 1 per cent of the housing starts on what would appear to be this cheaper one. Yet I think every one of us knows that this is one area of great need, namely that of low cost housing. It seems to me that these figures indicate that here has been an area of remarkable lack of success on the part of the legislation and on the part of the housing authority. I think we should have an explanation. Is it because the design is too ineffective? Is it not possible in our rural areas and in our small towns to get a house for $10,000? I would suggest to the minister that if the answer is yes, that these designs will not sell, that people will not take them, then we must consider further steps. But before I urge further steps I should like to have some remarks from the minister on those two matters.

The hon. member for St. James (Mr. Campeau) mentioned a few moments ago, if I remember rightly, that 22,000 housing units located in the city of Montreal, were built before 1870. This shows the urgency of eliminating those slums as soon as possible.
Earlier today the hon. member for St. James asked the government to find the means of urging cities to take advantage of the good offices of the C.M.H.C. During the 1957 session and again in 1958, I suggested to the minister that the government should contribute 75 per cent of the expropriation cost in the matter of slum clearance. The C.M.H.C. now contributes 50 per cent. Therefore, I urge the minister to take the required action so that the C.M.H.C. contribute 75 per cent of the expropriation cost of slums in order that cities such as Montreal and others may take advantage of the National Housing Act.
My riding is located in the oldest Montreal district, and I know something about slums. If the government increases the benefits provided by this act, it would surely be of advantage to the city of Montreal and allow the redevelopment of St. Ann riding. I know that at present the town planning committee of which I am a member, is conducting a complete survey in the western district of Montreal with a view to clearing slums and erecting new buildings.

Mr. Chairman, I renew the representations I made in the last sessions, to the effect that the government's share, in cases of expropriation, be raised to 75 per cent. Should such a decision be taken, a number of municipalities, even those smaller than Montreal, might avail themselves of the services of the C.M.H.C. I think it would be wise to carry out those works this year, while there is serious unemployment; it would provide jobs for the unemployed and would also allow municipalities to get rid of their slums.

Mr. Chairman, may I just make a suggestion to the Minister of Public Works, based on a brief submitted to the federal government on February 1, 1960 by the Canadian and Catholic Federation of Labour. On page 9, the brief reads as follows:

The absence of a working agreement at the present time-and indeed the absence of an agreement for a considerable period-is causing a hardship to other parts of Newfoundland outside of St. John's where housing developments are required. I understand there is some question whether under the present National Housing Act an agreement is not required before an arrangement can be worked out with an agent of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Perhaps I may interrupt to say that the only problem I know of was that in connection with this site in St. John's. We worked that out very nicely and had the co-operation of everyone in that regard. Has my hon. friend in mind any other agreement that is pending because of the litigation? I do not know of one from which we must stand aloof and not complete. We have already done a tremendous amount of building in St. John's. The people living in the units seem very pleased with them. I am talking now about the help given to the people. If there is a specific agreement to which my hon. friend has special reference I shall be glad to answer him.

It is the absence of an agreement about which I am talking. That is the problem. If there was an agreement we could go ahead. I understand that everything is at a standstill because there is no active agreement. All contractual arrangements have been suspended until this matter has been decided by the courts which may take some time. Because of that there is no agreement and there is no possibility of making any whereby housing developments can be carried out in Corner Brook and other urban areas.
I have in my hand the office consolidation of the National Housing Act, 1954, section 36 on page 38 which provides:
The corporation may, pursuant to agreements made between the government of Canada and the

government of any province, undertake jointly with the government of the province or any agency thereof works for the acquisition and development of land for housing purposes and for the construction of housing projects for sale or for rent.
The minister will recollect that earlier in the year I asked certain questions about the St. John's housing development in reply to which the minister informed me arrangements were being made to have the city of St. John's act as an agent of the provincial government. The provincial legislature has amended its legislation to make this possible but under this act it would appear that even though the provincial government does make the city its agent an agreement with the government is necessary.
An agreement with the province is a prerequisite before the federal government can carry out negotiations with an agent of the government. It is the lapse of time that is likely to take place before this litigation is determined in the courts that concerns me as well as the absence of an agreement and the standstill of housing developments until this matter is decided.
What I was hoping was that the government could say that it would let the dispute before the courts take its course but still enter into new agreements to permit housing developments to go ahead. That is what I had in mind. I did not take the time to elaborate as fully as I have now.

To follow up that subject, could the minister say if an attempt is being made to popularize or make better known this joint scheme between the federal and provincial governments and the municipalities?

Mr. Chairman, I presume I am the omega on these estimates. I want to express briefly my appreciation of the prompt and courteous way in which the senior officials of the corporation answer any correspondence and make things clear that were previously obscure to me. I also wish to say that a number of people in my district have expressed their appreciation of the very active way in which the representative of the corporation undertakes his duties and functions in the area. On a number of occasions I have gone with him to meet certain people and have found myself somewhat successful as a sort of mediator between the irate wife of a purchaser and a contractor. I usually find there is a little bit of wrong on both sides and so we have been able to come to a satisfactory conclusion. The representative of the corporation has been most anxious to do the best he can for people, particularly in settling difficult questions that are bound to arise when quite a number of houses are being built.
Having said that, may I say that I rose particularly to mention the fact that I have in my hand the report of the committee of inquiry into the design of the residential environment. This inquiry was undertaken under the auspices of the royal architectural institute of Canada and was made possible as a result of a grant from the federal government. I think it was a very wise investment. I am not

Supply-Public Works
going to deal with the report in detail tonight but I should like to ask the minister what the reaction of Central Mortgage and Housing [DOT]Corporation is to this report. There are a number of very excellent recommendations and I should like to refer particularly to the recommendation found in paragraph 201 which is in these terms:
The committee recommends to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, as the agency with a national mandate in housing and planning research, that it should convene a conference on the idea of a permanent Canadian institute of urban studies. The corporation need not in so doing commit itself in advance to this instrument. It should invite to the discussion the representatives of those governments, universities, national corporations and other research bodies that have already made significant contributions in urban studies in Canada.
I am particularly interested in that recommendation and I should like the minister to comment as to the reaction of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to the recommendations as a whole and particularly the one I have just read.

speechtext: I have just been informed by the president of the corporation that these recommendations are under active study at the present time by the corporation, and in due course I will be very happy to answer the inquiry of the hon. member.

Has the minister commented or is he going to comment on the matter I raised the other day having to do with greater federal aid in the construction of homes for senior citizens and for handicapped citizens?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We have made and will make loans for homes specially designed, for instance, for paraplegics. I know the abiding interest of the hon. member in this subject. He has ably followed in the footsteps of his father who was a pioneer in this field in the province of British Columbia.
Would the minister explain the details of the item as found on page 472? They are not very informative.

I do not know whether I heard the minister correctly earlier in the evening that there is a possibility that at the end of the year there may be a cut-back in the building of houses in Canada. Actually there has been a cut-back already during the summer months from the policy established at the beginning of the year. While I appreciate that the minister heeded the recommendation of members on this side of the house that the limit on loans should be extended and that some of the restrictions should be lifted, I am afraid that the minister has acted too late and with too little. Actually in most cases the $12,800 limit is

too low because it does not eliminate the necessity of having to secure second mortgages at a premium. That is what members of this party hoped would be accomplished. We hoped that the loan ceiling would be increased to eliminate the necessity of a great number of purchasers having to secure second mortgages at a premium and a high rate of interest.
I also deplore the fact that the minister has not given special consideration to the building of houses in rural areas because while there may not be large developments in rural areas it would be a great help both to the industry and to the people who live there if there were fewer restrictions.
I am also sorry that the minister did not find a formula to make it possible for people in the low income group to purchase homes. Even the raising of the present limit does not do much to aid people in the low income group because if a person is making less than $5,000 a year and has a family it is impossible for him to carry a mortgage of $12,800. Actually the greatest necessity with respect to housing is not necessarily houses that are pre-sold to people with higher incomes but houses for people with low incomes. Until such time as we succeed in doing that I feel the government is not doing all it can to assist the Canadian people to live in the manner that they should.
I am also sorry that the minister did not find some method whereby the cost of administration of C.M.H.C. might be credited to the lending institutions with the benefit of that credit going to the purchasers of homes who are in the low income group. While that has not been done this year, I would certainly appreciate it if the minister would take this matter into consideration for next year so that we will have some type of formula to make it easier for citizens in the low income group to purchase and carry the type of home that all Canadian citizens should have.

Mr. Chairman, we have no *quarrel with the National Capital Commission, because I believe it is pursuing the work so well started by the previous organization.
However, there are certain things which might stand improvement, as mentioned by the previous speaker. Thus the new style of government buildings to be erected in Ottawa :and the surrounding area, should be recon-
Supply-Public Works
sidered, because, in some cases we tend to modernize too much, whereas I believe that those buildings should remain in keeping with the parliament buildings, which give a character all its own to the city of Ottawa. As a matter of fact, people coming from the old capital of Quebec are quite struck with the ancient style which is perpetuated here. It gives the city a quite individual character and attracts people. I think that if we continue changing the style of federal buildings in Ottawa, we are going to destroy its attractiveness. We made a good start. If we had kept up the style of the Supreme Court and the Confederation buildings we would have preserved the character of our capital city, just as Quebec has its own style.
I think it would be to the advantage of the national capital, because tourists who come here from all over, and more particularly from the United States, want to see something different from what they have at home. In fact, this particular style would certainly attract them. Therefore, I think the previous speaker was quite right in asking the national capital commission to urge the federal government, as it has done in the past, to continue to adopt a particular style, even for buildings that must be built outside the area of government buildings.
I think that, in this connection, I have said enough, and in order not to take up too much of the time of the house, I shall now pass on to another matter.
The Expropriation Act creates particularly regrettable situations. With regard to commercial buildings, the Expropriation Act works very well because the commercial value that is, the general value of the business, is taken into account. But when it is a case of expropriating houses, small houses, built years ago, houses which have grown old with the people living in them, family houses, only the actual value of the house, less depreciation, is granted.
For instance, small houses have been expropriated, which were a little outside the limits of the municipality of Ottawa, where people lived happily on small pensions. Unfortunately, the expropriation cost was established on the basis of actual value of their houses, so they were granted an amount which did not allow them to find proper alternative accommodation, and they had to go and live in rental housing. Now, when people have grown old together on their old property, this becomes an important factor

Supply-Public Works
in their lives. Therefore, I think that the minister who is responsible for the national capital commission which is conducting many expropriations should suggest that the department revise the Expropriation Act, especially with regard to those one-unit houses that must disappear to make way for other buildings or even for the green belt that will surround the area.
This question has been raised before on various occasions and I think that as time passes it becomes increasingly necessary to take action. I understand that the present minister cannot change the situation by a stroke of the pen.
He cannot amend legislation in that way, but I am sure he could use his influence on his colleagues to improve the act so that people could receive a fairer amount.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with another subject.
Every spring the national capital commission used to take steps to control mosquitoes. This is quite important, because in the vicinity of the national capital, there are some swampy areas which serve as breeding grounds-
For Liberals.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps it would be the same elsewhere, but when the hon. member who has just spoken opens his mouth, I sometimes wonder whether that might be the source of all those mosquitoes.
In any event, Mr. Chairman, mosquitoes are the scourge of the national capital. In the past, it was customary-I am not sure whether that is still done, I am only asking- to spread oil over the swamps in the spring, to keep the mosquitoes under control. I do not know whether that has been done this year, but I know mosquitoes are a nuisance in the area, to such an extent that people cannot sit on their lawn at night, for fear of being eaten alive.
I therefore ask the minister responsible for the national capital commission to inquire from the members of the commission as to whether that procedure is to be continued.
I know that in the past, the municipalities concerned were asked to share in mosquito control measures by contributing a certain amount. This may seem funny to some members, but the situation creates a serious problem in the area. If these hon. gentle-

men had got around a bit in their lives, they would know that certain regions must face problems that do not exist elsewhere.
There are mosquitoes in my constituency too.

Just as we have.
Mr. Chairman, despite the interjections and dull jokes that we hear from a certain side of the house, I suggest this is an important problem, and I submit it to the minister in all sincerity.
Municipalities have been asked in the past to share in mosquito control. Some have refused to pay their share, and insecticides were sprayed elsewhere. But in the municipalities which had refused to pay, there were places especially favourable to the propagation of mosquitoes. The insects then spread to other areas, and at a meeting of the national capital commission, two years ago, we heard a representative of the town of Aylmer say that the mosquitoes they were fighting at the time were not those of Aylmer but those which had come from the national capital because they were much larger.
So, Mr. Chairman, I believe that the national capital commission should pay the cost of mosquito control because all the people in that area would benefit.

Mr. Chairman, I hope that the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) will forgive some of his collegues for having made fun of some of his remarks. If the question he raised brought a little bit of laughter, it is rather easy to understand at this late hour. He should perhaps blame himself too, because he possibly was not too clear about it. He referred to mosquitoes but he forgot to tell us if he was referring to the national capital mosquitoes or to those of the Liberal party.
In any event, Mr. Chairman, I should like to endorse the remarks the hon. member made about expropriations. I agree with the hon. member and, at the risk of being a little out of order, I would like to ask not only to the Minister of Public Works, but all the ministers who might be concerned with expropriation by the federal government, if it would not be appropriate to make a few changes not only in the application of the act, but also in the procedure of all the federal government departments and agencies.

With due humility, I ask the various departments conducting expropriations to urge the Department of Justice to look carefully into the whole expropriation system of the federal government, so that people who must suffer the inconvenience of an expropriation might have a better chance of being adequately compensated by the agencies or departments concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
In reply to the question of the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville and of the hon. member for Hull may I say that I think they both have made a very good point. We in this government believe, for the reasons stated by the hon. member for Hull and confirmed by the hon. member who has just spoken, that there should be more generous treatment for people who are living in modest homes, in frame houses, if they are going to be expropriated for this reason. Where are they going to get another place in which they can settle as cheaply?
Our department is represented on this committee at the present time. Of course, the Department of Justice will make the amendments. We are now in the process of contemplating a revision of the Expropriation Act. I am going to make a point of sending the speech of the hon. member for Hull and of the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville to that body, and I will leave out the part about the mosquitoes. This is very important. Let no one laugh at this.
I myself am living on the Rideau river and, believe me, in all my experience on survey parties in northern Ontario and elsewhere I have never found bigger or healthier mosquitoes. You will be glad to know that the campaign for the elimination of mosquitoes is a matter close to my heart. We contribute $6,000 a year and each of the municipalities is presently making a contribution including the city of Hull for which the hon. member who has just spoken is the member.

subtopic: MOTION FOR REFERENCE OF BILL NO. SD-314 TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters):
That the order for house again in committee of the whole on Bill No. SD-341, an act for the relief of Jacquelyn Gregory Bradley Walker be discharged and that the said bill be referred back to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills together with the evidence taken and the papers produced in respect of the said bill before the Senate standing committee on divorce.

subtopic: MOTION FOR REFERENCE OF BILL NO. SD-314 TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Will the hon. member indicate why this matter might not be left until the usual time tomorrow when the house would have an opportunity to know exactly what the purpose was?

subtopic: MOTION FOR REFERENCE OF BILL NO. SD-314 TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: This follows precisely the action taken by the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave), I believe on Thursday of last week with respect to another case of a similar nature which was transferred back for similar reasons, that case having received a great deal of publicity recently. This is in order to have it transferred as quickly as possible in view of the shortness of the session so that the steering committee can meet tomorrow and take action on it.

speechtext:
Would the house leader
indicate the business for Friday and Saturday?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
We will carry on with the estimates of the national capital commission, then take veterans affairs followed by northern affairs and national resources. These have been called before. If the house finishes those estimates we have available the estimates of secretary of state, defence production and legislation.
On Monday we will deal with legislative items which I will put before the house in more particular tomorrow, although we will be discussing Bill No. C-58, an act to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code. There may be one or two minor pieces of legislation which will be taken up before that but I will give the house due notice of that tomorrow.
